    • Fixed output
    • Filtered output
  • Configure releases and trigger timing
  • Monitor and test events
    • Recommended test sequence
  • Startup and runtime behavior
  • Worked examples
    • Hold a virtual button above a throttle detent
    • Send different shortcuts across a detent
    • Use the upper half of an axis for a full virtual-axis span
    • Select discrete axis presets with lever zones
  • Edit an existing layout safely
  • Troubleshooting

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Select an axis input in the profile and decide what should happen at each position. The action declares support for joystick-axis inputs; it is not a button or hat mapper.

Have the required output available before adding nested mappings:

  • For a virtual joystick output, know the destination device and axis or button.
  • For a keyboard command, know the shortcut the target application expects.
  • For a held output, decide what will release it.

Start with one interior gate and one simple action. Test that configuration before adding more boundaries or output behaviors.

Finalize the general gate layout before configuring many nested actions. Deleting gates or reducing the gate count can remove mappings from those gates and their adjacent ranges.

docs.title: Gates are positions; ranges are intervals
docs.text:
A gate is a particular axis value. A range is the interval between two neighboring gates.

For example:

Gate Position Low boundary -1.0 Detent 0.60 High boundary +1.0

These three gates define two ranges:

Range Bounds Possible use Lower range -1.0 to 0.60 Normal throttle travel Upper range 0.60 to +1.0 Boost or afterburner zone

Choose a gate condition when movement across a position should trigger a command. Choose a range condition when the position within an interval should control behavior.

docs.title: Normalized values and direction
docs.text:
The underlying axis values use -1.0 to +1.0:

  • -1.0: low end.
  • 0.0: center.
  • +1.0: high end.

An increasing crossing moves from a lower value to a higher value. A decreasing crossing moves from a higher value to a lower value. These describe numeric direction, not necessarily the physical forward/backward direction of your lever.

Move the control and watch its marker before assigning increasing/decreasing commands. Account for the axis processing in the profile rather than assuming a particular physical orientation.

docs.title: A range condition and an output mode are different
docs.text:
The condition tab determines when its nested actions run. The range's Output Mode determines how its continuous axis value is transformed.

For example, In Range with Rebased to [-1,1] sends a remapped axis value to its nested axis action. Range Hold instead supplies press/release events suitable for holding a virtual button or keyboard key.

docs.title: Create your first mapping
docs.text:
This example sends a command when an axis crosses a detent in the increasing direction.

  1. Select the source axis in the desired profile mode.
  2. Add Gated Axis to its action container.
  3. Move the physical control to the desired detent position.
  4. Select Add to create a gate at the live marker position.
  5. Double-click that gate's handle, or right-click it and select Configure....
  6. In the gate configuration dialog, select Condition: Cross (inc).
  7. Add a container and the required output action inside that tab.
  8. Configure the nested action's output. For example, use Keyboard Ex in Pulse mode to send a short command.
  9. Close the configuration dialog and save the profile.
  10. Move across the gate in both directions while observing the event display.
  11. Start the profile and confirm that the target application receives the intended command.

The increasing condition should respond when the axis crosses from below the gate to above it. Moving back uses the decreasing direction, which can have a different mapping.

docs.title: Add a gate at the physical control position
docs.text: Move the axis until the live marker is at the desired position, then select Add. This is useful for matching a physical detent.

docs.title: Add a gate at a chosen slider position
docs.text:
Right-click the range on the slider and select Add Gate.... The new gate is added at the clicked position.

Duplicate positions are rejected or marked as conflicts. Keep neighboring gates separated so each range has usable width.

docs.title: Move a gate
docs.text:
Drag its slider handle or edit its value in the gate row. The gate row also provides a grab control for capturing the current source position.

After repositioning a gate, verify both adjacent ranges. Changing a boundary changes which physical positions belong to each range.

docs.title: Set the gate count
docs.text:
Enter the required total in Set gate count, then select Set.

  • The editor supports at least 2 gates and a maximum of 20 in the current implementation.
  • The count includes the low and high boundary gates. Three ordered gates normally define two adjacent ranges.
  • Reducing the count prompts for confirmation because it can remove gate configurations and normalize positions.

Use the actual range rows shown by the editor to confirm the resulting layout.

docs.title: Normalize positions
docs.text:
Control Effect Normalize Spaces gates evenly over the existing outer-gate range. Normalize (reset) Uses the full axis range and spaces gates evenly across it.

Normalization changes gate positions. Do it before tuning detents to a particular physical device, or recheck those positions afterward.

docs.title: Display Mode
docs.text:
The standard action widget offers Normal and Percent displays. The shared widget can also expose other labels when embedded elsewhere.

Display Mode controls the representation of values. It is separate from the range Output Mode and does not, by itself, select an output mapping or change its behavior. Examples in this guide use normalized values to avoid ambiguity.

docs.title: Configure gate-crossing actions
docs.text:
Open a gate through its configuration control, by double-clicking its slider handle, or through the right-click Configure... command.

Use Gate Description to give it a meaningful name, such as “Idle detent” or “Boost threshold.” Add containers/actions separately on the condition tabs you need.

Gate condition When it triggers Example Crossed The axis crosses the gate in either direction. A notification at a detent. Cross (inc) The axis crosses from a lower value toward a higher value. Enable a function above a threshold. Cross (dec) The axis crosses from a higher value toward a lower value. Disable a function on the return movement.

A crossing is an event, not a held state. Remaining on one side of a gate does not create repeated crossing events unless the axis crosses it again.

Do not put the same one-shot command on both Crossed and Cross (inc) unless you want both mappings to run on an increasing crossing. Each tab has its own mapping.

For a momentary output from a crossing, choose either a nested action that handles its own timed release or configure the gate's Autorelease behavior. See Configure releases and trigger timing.

docs.title: Configure range actions
docs.text:
Double-click the space between gate handles, use a range's configuration control, or right-click the range and select Configure....

Set a Range Description, then choose the relevant condition tab.

Range condition Meaning Suitable use In Range Supplies axis-value updates while the source is inside the interval. Drive a virtual axis using this part of the input travel. Enter Range Generates an activation when the source enters the interval. Send a one-shot command on entry. Exit Range Generates an activation when the source leaves the interval. Send a one-shot command on exit. Range Hold Press on entry; release on exit. Hold a virtual button or keyboard command while in the zone. Outside of Range Processes updates while the source is outside this interval. Specialized outside-state behavior.

docs.title: In Range: continuous value mapping
docs.text:
Use this tab when the nested action needs an axis value. Its Output Mode controls whether that value is unchanged, scaled, fixed, rebased, or filtered.

Add an axis-capable action, such as Map to vJoy configured for an axis destination. Set the destination inside that nested action; defining the range alone does not choose an output device.

In Range responds to incoming value changes. It is not a periodic timer that repeatedly runs a command while the axis is stationary.

docs.title: Enter Range and Exit Range: one-shot events
docs.text:
Both conditions produce activation events. Exit Range is not a key-up event for an Enter Range action. It is a separate condition with its own mappings.

For example, put a Keyboard Ex Pulse action on Enter Range to send one shortcut, and a different Pulse action on Exit Range to send another.

If you want a single output held throughout the interval, use Range Hold instead of trying to pair unrelated entry and exit containers.

docs.title: Range Hold: matched press and release
docs.text:
Use Range Hold with an output action that follows button state:

  1. Select Condition: Range Hold.
  2. Add a container and a button-capable output action.
  3. For a virtual button, configure a normal hold mapping to the destination button.
  4. For a keyboard key, configure Keyboard Ex in Hold mode.
  5. Move into and out of the interval and verify both output states.

This condition supplies the natural release when the axis leaves. It does not need a timed release to simulate the end of a crossing pulse.

docs.title: Outside of Range
docs.text:
This condition can process many input updates while the axis remains outside the interval. It is not equivalent to “fire once when exiting.” Use Exit Range for a one-shot exit command.

In the reviewed handler, Outside of Range events carry a released/false button state, and the editor exposes a button-type mapping on this tab. Check the nested action's execution settings; a press-only mapping may not react. Use Range Hold for the common “on inside, off outside” requirement.

docs.title: Choose a range output mode
docs.text:
The following settings are available on a range's In Range tab.

Output Mode Value sent to nested axis actions Normal The input axis value, unchanged. Output Fixed Value The configured Fixed Value while inside the interval. Ranged The position within this interval, scaled to Range Min and Range Max. Filtered (no output) Suppresses the regular in-range axis-value output. Rebased to [-1,1] Maps this interval's low boundary to -1.0 and high boundary to +1.0.

docs.title: Normal versus rebased values
docs.text:
Suppose a range runs from 0.60 to 1.00:

Source position Normal output Rebased output 0.60 0.60 -1.00 0.80 0.80 0.00 1.00 1.00 +1.00

Use Normal to preserve the source's position. Use Rebased when a small part of the physical travel should operate a complete virtual-axis span.

docs.title: Ranged scaling
docs.text:
Select Ranged, then enter Range Min and Range Max under Scaling options.

For a physical interval of 0.60 to 1.00, output limits of 0.00 and 1.00 produce:

Source position Ranged output 0.60 0.00 0.80 0.50 1.00 1.00

The range dialog's Reset restores its scaling limits to that interval's input bounds. It does not necessarily select -1.0 to +1.0. Choose Rebased or explicitly enter full-span limits when that is what you want.

docs.title: Fixed output
docs.text:
Select Output Fixed Value and enter the required value. This is useful for mapping a lever position zone to a discrete axis setting, such as a flap preset.

The value is an output to nested actions; it does not physically lock the source control. Outside the zone, another mapping must define any subsequent output you require.

docs.title: Filtered output
docs.text:
Use Filtered (no output) when this range should not pass its normal axis-value stream to nested actions.

Filtering is not a command to set an output to zero or release a key. The destination can retain its previous value. Gate crossings and other configured range conditions are separate from the continuous axis-value output, so review those tabs as well.

docs.title: Configure releases and trigger timing
docs.text:
Gate-crossing tabs and range Enter/Exit tabs expose Autorelease. The configuration dialog also has Trigger Delay, in milliseconds.

With Autorelease enabled, a trigger is followed by a release after the delay. This lets a crossing or entry event behave like a short button press for a nested action that expects a down/up pair.

Trigger Delay is not a dwell time, gate-crossing sensitivity, or noise filter. It does not require the axis to stay beyond a gate before activating the command.

Choose the release strategy that matches the task:

Task Suggested setup Hold a button while in a zone Range Hold plus a nested hold-style output. Brief key command at a crossing Gate condition plus Keyboard Ex Pulse. Make a crossing resemble a momentary button Gate condition with Autorelease, plus an action that follows the generated button state. Separate commands on entering and leaving Different one-shot actions on Enter Range and Exit Range.

If a nested action has its own pulse duration, distinguish that duration from Gated Axis Trigger Delay. Adding two independent release mechanisms can make diagnosis harder; begin with the one your output actually needs.

docs.title: Monitor and test events
docs.text:
Enable Show events to display Range events and Gate events. Use the event-type checkboxes to reduce clutter:

  • All selects every event type for display.
  • None hides all event types from these lists.
  • Individual checkboxes select the displayed categories.

These are display filters. They do not disable the action mappings. Likewise, hiding Show events does not turn off the Gated Axis action.

The reviewed handler keeps a short rolling history of the latest events rather than a permanent event log. These display histories are populated for editor-time diagnostics; do not assume they are a complete runtime execution trace.

docs.title: Recommended test sequence
docs.text:
1. With the profile stopped, move the axis slowly through every range.
  2. Cross each configured gate in the increasing direction.
  3. Cross it again in the decreasing direction.
  4. Pause on each side and watch for unexpected repeated crossings.
  5. Test the low and high ends and positions close to each boundary.
  6. Start the profile and verify the actual virtual/key output.
  7. Test a fast sweep, startup at several positions, and relevant runtime-mode changes.

An event appearing in the editor confirms trigger detection. It does not, by itself, prove that the nested action has a valid destination or that the target application accepts its output.

docs.title: Startup and runtime behavior
docs.text:
After profile startup, the action reads the current axis position and sends an initialization event to the gate handler. You do not necessarily have to move the control before range-related actions become active.

The reviewed handler's first evaluation can initialize:

  • Enter Range and Range Hold for ranges containing the current value.
  • Exit Range and outside-state behavior for other ranges.

Consequently, a one-shot mapped to Enter Range or Exit Range can run at startup without a physical crossing. Test startup separately, particularly when those commands have lasting effects. Do not assume “Exit Range” always proves the axis previously occupied that range during the current run.

Unchanged axis values are skipped by the trigger processor. Normal axis updates drive the evaluation; Gated Axis is not a repeating command timer.

A fast change can cross several gates between samples and produce several crossing events. Do not depend on their delivery order for a tightly timed command sequence. Configure a sequence action if strict ordering is required.

The action participates in profile-mode handling. If behavior changes after a mode switch, verify the active mode, its inherited mappings, and the nested action's conditions.

docs.title: Hold a virtual button above a throttle detent
docs.text:
1. Add an interior gate at 0.80.
  2. Open the upper range, 0.80 to 1.00.
  3. Select Condition: Range Hold.
  4. Add Map to vJoy with a normal button-hold mapping to the required destination button.
  5. Save, start the profile, and move across the detent in both directions.

Expected result: the virtual button is on while the throttle is in the upper zone and off after it leaves. Verify the exact boundary and startup position on your device.

docs.title: Send different shortcuts across a detent
docs.text:
1. Add a gate at the desired threshold, such as 0.50.
  2. Open Condition: Cross (inc) and add Keyboard Ex Pulse with the command for increasing travel.
  3. Open Condition: Cross (dec) and add a second Pulse action with the command for decreasing travel.
  4. Leave Crossed empty unless a separate both-directions command is also required.
  5. Test the actual command sent in each direction.

Use the condition-tab names and the direction of the live axis value when testing. The event history has a direction-label issue in the reviewed handler; see the version notes below.

docs.title: Use the upper half of an axis for a full virtual-axis span
docs.text:
1. Create gates at -1.0, 0.0, and 1.0.
  2. Open the upper range's In Range tab.
  3. Select Rebased to [-1,1].
  4. Add Map to vJoy in Absolute axis mode and choose the destination axis.
  5. Move from just above 0.0 to 1.0 and verify full virtual travel.

Normal output on that interval would use only 0.0 to 1.0; rebasing expands the interval to the full normalized span. Configure the lower range separately. If it is filtered, the destination may retain its last value while the source is there.

docs.title: Select discrete axis presets with lever zones
docs.text:
1. Add gates to divide the travel into the desired zones.
  2. On each range's In Range tab, select Output Fixed Value.
  3. Enter a different output value for each zone, such as -1.0, 0.0, and +1.0 for three zones.
  4. Add a Map to vJoy axis action in each zone, all targeting the intended axis.
  5. Check each zone and start the profile with the lever in different positions.

Expected result: the virtual axis receives the configured preset for the occupied zone. Use descriptions to keep the zones recognizable after editing.

docs.title: Edit an existing layout safely
docs.text:
Before deleting or substantially repositioning gates, save the profile and preserve important mappings using the application's duplication, template, or clipboard features where available.

To delete a gate, right-click its handle and select Delete Gate, or use the gate-row delete control. The editor prevents deletion below two gates and can prompt when the gate or adjacent ranges contain mappings.

Removing a gate changes the adjacent intervals. Reopen those ranges and check their condition tabs and output modes afterward. Do the same after reducing the gate count or normalizing the layout.

The editor provides a Ctrl+Z snapshot undo mechanism while the profile is stopped and UI key input is not suspended. The history is limited to 20 snapshots. Do not treat it as complete undo coverage for every gate operation or nested action edit; saving a known-good profile remains the dependable recovery point.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text: Symptom Check Moving the axis produces no output The intended condition tab contains an action; the profile is running in the correct mode; nested conditions are satisfied; its output destination is valid. Gates move, but commands never run Editing a layout alone does not add output actions. Open the gate/range and configure a container on the relevant condition tab. A command repeats throughout a zone A continuous In Range or Outside of Range condition may be driving it. Use Enter Range or Exit Range for a one-shot. A button remains pressed after leaving Use Range Hold with a hold-style nested action, or provide an appropriate timed/explicit release for a crossing action. Exit Range does not release the Enter Range output Exit Range is a separate activation. Use Range Hold for matched press/release behavior. Output uses only part of a virtual axis Use Rebased or Ranged rather than Normal; also check scaling in the nested action. Filtered range leaves the last output in place Expected: filtering suppresses updates; it does not reset the destination. Configure a fixed value or another condition if a reset is required. Direction appears backward Check numeric movement and the chosen Cross (inc)/(dec) tab. Account for the event-history label issue noted below. Small movement triggers a gate repeatedly Observe whether the input oscillates across the boundary; reposition the gate away from an unstable rest position or address source-axis processing. Trigger Delay is not a deadband. One crossing causes duplicate commands Check Crossed and directional tabs, adjacent range Enter/Exit mappings, and other actions on the same source. Startup sends an unexpected command The initialization evaluation can fire range conditions without movement. Test the initial position and review Enter/Exit mappings. Mapping information disappeared after editing Gate deletion, gate-count reduction, or normalization may have changed affected ranges. Restore the saved profile or preserved mapping. Cannot add a gate Check for an existing gate at that value and the 20-gate maximum. Range cannot be configured sensibly Separate coincident gates and check adjacent boundaries. No event-history text Enable Show events and at least one display filter; test in the editor. The history is not a complete runtime log. Analog output looks scaled twice Review the range Output Mode and the nested action's own range/curve processing.

docs.title: Keyboard Ex — User Guide
docs.text:
Map to Keyboard/Mouse Ex converts an input into a keyboard combination, mouse-button action, or mouse-wheel event. Use it to hold a command while a joystick button is down, send a timed shortcut, repeat a command, or control when an output is pressed and released.

This guide describes the Map to Keyboard/Mouse EX action. Shared dialogs and process-routing options may have different wording in another build.

docs.title: Contents
docs.text:
• Keyboard Ex — User Guide
  • Contents
  • Before you start
    • A combination is not a typing sequence
  • Create your first mapping
  • Choose keys and mouse inputs
    • Record a shortcut
    • Select a shortcut visually
  • Choose an output mode
    • Hold
    • Press and Release
    • Pulse
    • AutoRepeat
    • Toggle
  • Set duration and interval
  • Choose the triggering event
  • Use mouse buttons and the wheel
    • Mouse buttons
    • Mouse wheel
  • Set the startup state
  • Choose local, remote, or process output
    • Normal local output
    • Remote output
    • Target a process
  • Worked examples
    • Hold a push-to-talk key
    • Send one shortcut
    • Repeat an adjustment while held
    • Separate “on” and “off” controls
    • Send a command when a button is released
  • Test and troubleshoot

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Have a profile containing the source input and know the key or mouse command expected by the target application.

The action advertises support for joystick buttons and hats. Hat inputs require a virtual-button activation condition so the action receives an on/off state. Configure the required hat direction in the surrounding input/container controls.

The implementation also requests virtual-button activation for axis inputs that reach it, but axes are not in its declared action input list. Do not assume you can add it directly to a raw axis in every build.

For your first test:

  • Choose one source button.
  • Use one output key.
  • Leave process targeting off and test local output with the intended application focused.
  • Keep State on profile start set to Ignore.

docs.title: A combination is not a typing sequence
docs.text:
The keys shown under Current key combination form a group of outputs. For example, Ctrl + Shift + A is one shortcut, not three separately timed keystrokes, like a macro or sequence would be.

The action sorts its keys for pressing and releases them in reverse order. Recording multiple inputs does not preserve typing pauses or create a timed macro. Use a sequence/macro action if you need “press A, wait, then press B.”

Put together, the keys that make up a shortcut are called latched keys. They can be pressed in any order, but to trigger, they must all be pressed at the same time.

docs.title: Create your first mapping
docs.text:
1. Select the profile mode and source joystick button.
  2. Add Map to Keyboard/Mouse Ex to its action container.
  3. Select Select... and choose the output key, or use the single-input listen control.
  4. Confirm that the key appears under Current key combination.
  5. Select Hold under Output Mode.
  6. Leave the trigger configured for input press rather than release-only operation.
  7. Save and start the profile.
  8. Focus the target application, hold the source button, and then release it.
  9. Confirm that the output activates while held and stops when released.

To send a brief command instead of following the source button's state, change Output Mode to Pulse and set Duration (ms).

docs.title: Choose keys and mouse inputs
docs.text: Control Use Single-input listen Capture one output input through the listener. Listen (multi) Capture multiple keyboard or mouse inputs; confirm with OK when finished. Select... Choose keys through the virtual-keyboard dialog. This is often the fastest and easiest option to select keys Clear Remove the current output selection. Right-click an output key, then Delete Remove that key from the combination.

docs.title: Record a shortcut
docs.text:
1. Select Listen (multi).
  2. Enter the shortcut you want to send, such as Ctrl + Shift + A.
  3. Select OK in the listener.
  4. Review the resulting combination before testing it.

The listener's tooltip states that clicks on its dialog buttons are excluded from the recorded selection. It accepts keyboard and mouse inputs.

docs.title: Select a shortcut visually
docs.text:
1. Select Select....
  2. Choose the required keys in the virtual keyboard.
  3. Accept the dialog.
  4. Check the displayed combination.

This method is the easiest and preferred method to select (or deselect) keys, as it lets you also pick keys that may not exist on your keyboard/input device. For example, the media keys, the F13 to F24 keys, or all mouse buttons and horizontal wheel triggers, may all be hard to input using the listen mode. This is also difficult if your keyboard is not a 100% sized keyboard, does not have a numeric keypad or combines multiple keys like a 60% keyboard. The visual keyboard includes all standard keys, including many that are not on a normal keyboard but can be output to a game.

Pay attention to left/right modifiers or extended or numpad keys when the target application distinguishes them. These keys report as different keys even if they normally produce the same output (a good example of that would be the home key or the multiply or enter keys).

For ordinary output mappings, select at least one key or mouse input.

docs.title: Choose an output mode
docs.text: Mode Result Use it for Hold Presses the combination while the source is on; releases it when the source turns off. Push-to-talk, momentary controls, or dragging with a mouse button. Press Sends key-down or mouse-button-down without an automatic matching release. One control starts a held command. Release Sends key-up or mouse-button-up for the selected outputs. A second control ends a held command. Pulse Presses the combination, holds it for Duration, then releases it. Shortcuts and single commands. AutoRepeat Repeatedly presses and releases the combination while the source is active. Repeated adjustment or navigation. Toggle Changes each selected output to the opposite of its observed pressed state. Alternating a held command on and off.

docs.title: Hold
docs.text:
Hold follows the source input's state. Keep a normal source release path available so the output can be released.

The action does not generate its own repeat pulses in Hold mode. If you need deliberate press/release repetition, use AutoRepeat. How the receiving application interprets a continuously held key is separate from this action's repeat behavior.

docs.title: Press and Release
docs.text:
Treat these as a pair when creating a persistent output:

  1. Configure one source with Press and the desired combination.
  2. Configure another source with Release and the same combination.
  3. Verify both actions use the same output destination.
  4. Test starting and ending the held command.

Releasing the source that triggered Press does not automatically send key-up. Stopping the profile does not provide the same explicit held-key cleanup for Press as it does for Hold.

docs.title: Pulse
docs.text:
Pulse sends one timed press/release. Its duration is independent of how long you hold the source button. In this implementation, an ordinary source release does not cancel a running one-shot pulse.

While a pulse is already running, another request for that same action is ignored. For rapid successive commands, choose a duration short enough to finish before the next trigger, or consider AutoRepeat.

docs.title: AutoRepeat
docs.text:
AutoRepeat pulses the selected combination while the source is active. Source release stops the pulse worker. Profile stop and runtime-mode changes also request that the worker stop.

Use the normal press-triggered configuration. The editor warns against execute-on-release operation for this mode; a release-only configuration does not provide the intended start/stop cycle.

docs.title: Toggle
docs.text:
Toggle checks the current observed state of each selected output and sends the opposite state. It is not a single stored on/off flag for the entire combination.

For predictable results, start with a single output key or mouse button. When toggling a combination, physical keys or other mappings can leave different members in different states. Provide a Release action if you need a definite “all selected outputs off” command.

docs.title: Set duration and interval
docs.text:
Timing controls use milliseconds.

Setting Applies to Meaning Duration (ms) Pulse and AutoRepeat How long the outputs remain pressed during a pulse. Interval (ms) AutoRepeat The pause between pulses.

For example, a Duration of 100 ms and Interval of 200 ms describe a brief press followed by a longer gap. Use these as example values, not fixed product defaults.

New actions take their timing values from the application's last-used keyboard-mapper settings. Changing a timing value updates that preference. Do not assume every new action starts at 250 ms or another fixed value.

If the target application misses a command, increase Duration. If repetition is too fast, increase Interval. Test with the target application before choosing very short timings.

docs.title: Choose the triggering event
docs.text:
The execution controls choose whether supported actions activate on the source press, release, or both.

For most mappings, begin with:

  • Execute on press: enabled.
  • Execute on release: disabled.

For Press, Release, Pulse, and Toggle, a qualifying source release can be used as the activation event. A Release output action triggered by a source press is also valid: the output operation and the source event are separate choices.

For example, selecting Pulse with execute on release sends a short shortcut when you let go of the source button.

Enabling both press and release can produce two activations per physical cycle. Avoid that for toggles or commands you want to send only once.

Hold and AutoRepeat need special care. The editor warns against execute-on-release use for both. Hold's runtime path follows input state directly rather than acting as a release-triggered one-shot. AutoRepeat should start on press and stop on release.

docs.title: Use mouse buttons and the wheel
docs.text:
Keyboard Ex can include mouse buttons and wheel events in its output selection as a convenience. It does not provide cursor-position or cursor-motion configuration. The mouse buttons and wheel events are momentary events as well like other keys, which makes them particularly suitable to be mapped in this action. It is also helpful to include mouse functions with other latched keys such as the usual modifier (shift or alt or ctrl, but also other keys. For example in GEX, you can create a shortcut that includes left ctrl + right shift + A + mouse 5.

Internally, GEX creates special keys for these inputs and translates them to mouse output for the game / application to use, even if they appear in this action as keyboard keys. This is a visual, convenience representation, not a special translation GEX does.

docs.title: Mouse buttons
docs.text:
Use the listener to select the desired mouse input, then choose its behavior:

  • Hold keeps the button down while the source is held.
  • Pulse produces a timed down/up pair.
  • Press and Release let separate sources control the down and up operations.
  • Toggle changes the observed button state.

If the combination includes a keyboard modifier and a mouse button, test the complete interaction in the target application.

docs.title: Mouse wheel
docs.text:
Select the desired wheel direction and set Mouse Wheel Factor. The field accepts values from 1 to 100, with a supplied default of 1.

The factor controls wheel movement per trigger. It does not select a repeat rate. Start at 1 and increase it only after verifying the direction and amount.

In this version, the direct mouse-output paths pass the wheel factor explicitly, but the Pulse and AutoRepeat paths do not pass that action setting. Do not assume the factor scales wheel output identically in every mode. Verify timed wheel output before relying on it.

docs.title: Set the startup state
docs.text:
State on profile start offers Ignore and Input behavior.

Choice Behavior Ignore Does not issue an output merely to synchronize with the source at startup. This is the supplied default. Input Reads the source state and processes a corresponding input event when the profile starts.

For joystick buttons, the action reads whether the button is held. For hats, it reads the current hat state; the surrounding direction/activation setup still matters.

Input synchronization uses the selected output mode. It can therefore press a key, start a timed operation, or toggle an output when the startup event qualifies. It is not limited to Hold.

Use Ignore when starting the profile should not send a command. Test Input synchronization with the source both held and released before using it in a regular profile. The supplied startup routine does not sample an axis position for this action.

docs.title: Choose local, remote, or process output
Normal local output
docs.text:
Without process targeting, the action uses the focused-window target for keyboard output. Focus the intended application before the first test.

Check the action's output-routing controls if the source triggers but no local output appears. The selected route must include local output for a local test.

docs.title: Remote output
docs.text:
Use the remote-client controls to choose the intended recipients. The action obtains its client list when the profile starts and passes routing information to its send routines.

Configure the application's remote connection first. When diagnosing a remote mapping, verify the same key locally, then verify the chosen client and routing settings.

docs.title: Target a process
docs.text:
The process-target controls let the action look for a configured process/window instead of using the default keyboard target.

  1. Start the target application.
  2. Configure the target process in the action's process controls.
  3. Choose exact or partial matching as appropriate to the shared selector.
  4. Start the profile so the action performs its process lookup.
  5. Test a simple key before using a larger combination.

For local process output, failure to find the target window disables this action's output. The target is looked up during profile startup, not rediscovered for every input event. If the application was absent, fix the selection and restart or reload the profile to reinitialize the action; check the log if output remains disabled.

Do not assume mouse output follows the same process-target path as keyboard output. Direct mouse-button sends do not carry the same target-window information. Test mouse behavior separately.

Process-name and partial-match metadata are also passed with supported remote keyboard sends so the remote side can resolve its target. The behavior of the shared process selector and receiver is outside this action file.

docs.title: Hold a push-to-talk key
docs.text:
1. Add Keyboard Ex to the desired joystick button.
  2. Select the target application's push-to-talk key, such as F10.
  3. Choose Hold.
  4. Leave startup state at Ignore for the first test.
  5. Start the profile and test the source press and release.

Expected result: F10 is held while the source is held and released when the source is released.

docs.title: Send one shortcut
docs.text:
1. Select Ctrl + Shift + A using Select... or Listen (multi).
  2. Choose Pulse.
  3. Set Duration to 120 ms.
  4. Enable execute on press only.
  5. Test in an application where that shortcut has the intended effect.

Expected result: one activation presses the combination, waits for the duration, and releases it in reverse order.

docs.title: Repeat an adjustment while held
docs.text:
1. Select the adjustment key expected by the target application.
  2. Choose AutoRepeat.
  3. Begin with Duration 80 ms and Interval 250 ms.
  4. Use execute on press, then verify that releasing the source stops the output.
  5. Adjust the timings to suit the receiving application.

These timings are example starting values, not product defaults.

docs.title: Separate “on” and “off” controls
docs.text:
1. On the first source, select the required output and choose Press.
  2. On the second source, select the same output and choose Release.
  3. Match their routing and process settings.
  4. Activate the first source, then the second.

Expected result: the first source holds the output on; the second explicitly releases it.

docs.title: Send a command when a button is released
docs.text:
1. Select the desired shortcut.
  2. Choose Pulse.
  3. Disable execute on press and enable execute on release.
  4. Set the duration and test a full source press/release cycle.

Expected result: the shortcut is sent when the source is released. Do not substitute Hold or AutoRepeat for this release-triggered one-shot setup.

docs.title: Test and troubleshoot
docs.text:
Test a simple key first, then the complete combination. Verify press, hold, release, startup, runtime-mode change, and profile stop where relevant to the chosen output mode.

You may find it helpful to not test your keyboard/mouse output to the game directly, but to an application that repeats these keys for you. One example is the Thrustmaster key/event tester that comes with the Thrusmaster control software. Another is this utility keyboard key info. The utility shoudl be able to handle non-standard keystrokes and mouse input - as a normal text editor may not understand some keys, not display them, or ignore them.

Symptom Check No output Profile running; correct runtime mode; action/container conditions; nonempty key selection; output routing; target window/process. Output goes to the wrong application Focused window, configured process target, process match, and selected remote client. Action stops working after a process lookup failure Start the target, correct the process selection, and reinitialize the action by restarting/reloading the profile. Key remains held Press or Toggle mode, absent Release action, missing source release event, or an activation condition that never returns off. Hold does not generate repeated commands Hold does not create repeat pulses; use AutoRepeat when repeated down/up events are required. Repeat continues after letting go Source release reaches the action; normal press-triggered AutoRepeat configuration; no other action generating the same output. Command fires twice Both source press and release enabled, repeated source events, or duplicate mappings. GEX triggers keys twice, once on press (make), and once on release (break). Rapid presses are missed in Pulse mode The previous pulse may still be running; shorten Duration or revise the desired repeat behavior. Target misses brief commands Increase Duration and test again. Some games may not poll keyboard/mouse input rapidly enough, and conversely, some games treat everything as a trigger. Some games may consider 100 or 125 millisecond a short tap, and anything above 150 a long tap, which may change the behavior of the game. Target does not trigger Ensure that a key, if pressed, is released at some point. Keeping a key pressed may lock up of freeze the game, and even the operating system because it's waiting for a release. You can have a press in one action, a release in another, but you should aim to release every key you have sent as a press by the time the profile stops. You can clear a key that is stuck in pressed mode by pressing it again on the physical keyboard, which will send a release. This may not be possible for special keys if they don't exist on your keyboard in which case you'll have to code the profile for that. Wheel movement is excessive Reduce Mouse Wheel Factor; start at 1. Check repeat settings separately. Some mouse drivers may accelerate the mouse differently and in some implementations, using high DPI resolution can impact the response of the wheel. Wheel factor appears ignored in a timed mode Pulse/AutoRepeat do not explicitly pass the factor in this version. Shortcut becomes separate letters Review the selected modifier combination, output mode, other mappings, and actual target. Toggle combination reaches a mixed state Toggle checks individual key states; use Release to establish a definite off state. Starting the profile sends a command State on profile start is Input and the startup event qualifies under the chosen mode. Use Ignore if that is unwanted. Hat mapping triggers in the wrong direction Review the surrounding virtual-button activation/direction configuration.

To recover during testing, release the source and stop the profile. For Press or Toggle outputs, use the configured Release action rather than assuming profile stop releases everything.

docs.title: Map to State — User Guide
docs.text:
Map to State changes the profile's ordinary on/off states from an input. Use it to follow a physical switch, toggle a flag, send a pulse, select a control bank, or update a set of related states.

Create and organize states in the State Device. Map inputs to ordinary states, then use those states or derived expression states in conditions, State containers, and output mappings.

docs.title: Contents
docs.text:
• Create your first mapping
  • Choose the target states
  • One state
  • An explicit list
  • Categories
  • Attributes
  • Follow a switch or held button
  • Set or clear a state
  • Toggle a state
  • Pulse a state
  • Latch a state for a fixed interval
  • Choose the triggering event
  • Apply an operation to other states
  • Map a hat to states
  • Use randomized state changes
  • Startup and stop settings
  • Worked examples
  • Track a panel switch
  • Trigger one state from another
  • Use a state as a condition
  • Toggle an alternate command layer
  • Clear a group of flags
  • Select one state in a category
  • Test the mapping

docs.title: Create your first mapping
docs.text:
1. Create an ordinary state named shift_held in the State Device, with Default State set to Off.
  2. Select a physical button and add Map to State to its action container.
  3. Under Apply to, choose State (single).
  4. Select shift_held in State.
  5. Select Hold under Mode.
  6. Leave Other State Mode on NoOp and Randomize disabled.
  7. Save and start the profile.
  8. Watch shift_held in the input viewer while pressing and releasing the source.

Hold sends the source's pressed/released value to the state. The state should be On while the button is held and Off after release.

The action offers button, hat, and keyboard input types according to the surrounding input configuration. Start with a joystick button when testing a new state setup. A raw hat uses the direction table described below.

docs.title: Choose the target states
docs.text: Apply to selects the states changed by the action's main Mode. Use ordinary states for these targets. Expression states should get their values from their source states.

docs.title: One state
docs.text:
Choose State (single), then select the state by name. The Description field helps identify its purpose.

The adjacent add control creates a state without leaving the action. In Add State, enter a unique name, optional description, and an On or Off default. Confirm, then check the action's selected state. Use the full State Editor for expressions, categories, attributes, autorelease, or exclusive groups.

docs.title: An explicit list
docs.text:
Choose States (multi). Click Pick… in the States list and select the names to include. Select list entries and click Remove to remove them from this action's target list.

The main operation applies to every listed target. For example, Release (off) can clear a fixed list of flags with one input.

docs.title: Categories
docs.text:
Choose Category, click Pick… beside Categories, and select one or more categories. The action matches states in any of the selected categories.

Review Impacted states before testing. Assigning another state to a selected category adds it to that selection without adding its name to an explicit list.

docs.title: Attributes
docs.text:
Choose Attributes, then use Pick… to choose labels defined on states. A state matches if it has any of the selected attributes; it does not need all of them.

Use exact attribute spelling and case. Check Impacted states after changing the selection or editing state labels. For example, attach reset_on_command to flags in several categories, then target that attribute from one reset action.

For Category and Attributes, keep expression states out of the writable selection by choosing suitable categories or labels. Use an expression when the requirement is a logical combination of state values.

docs.title: Follow a switch or held button
docs.text:
Select Hold when the state should follow the physical input. Hold handles the source's On and Off values, so it is appropriate for a maintained switch or a temporary shift button.

Select Invert when a pressed source should set the state Off and a released source should set it On. Start with Execute on press enabled and verify both edges in the viewer.

Ensure the surrounding container and conditions let release events reach the mapping. For a maintained switch, also set startup synchronization to Input so an already-on switch is read when the profile starts.

docs.title: Set or clear a state
docs.text:
Use Press (on) to set the targets On when the selected event triggers. Use Release (off) to set them Off. These names describe the requested state value; Execute on press/release selects the physical event that performs the operation.

For separate On and Off controls:

  1. Add Map to State to the On input, select the target, and choose Press (on).
  2. Add another to the Off input, select the same target, and choose Release (off).
  3. Use execution on press only for both actions.
  4. Test the two controls in either order.

Setting an ordinary state to its existing value normally does not create a new state transition. Use Pulse for a momentary event or change the state deliberately when its attached actions need another press/release cycle.

docs.title: Toggle a state
docs.text:
Select Toggle to change Off to On or On to Off on each qualifying event. New actions use Toggle with execution on press only.

For a one-button switch, keep Execute on press enabled and Execute on release disabled. Test two complete press/release cycles: the first press should set the state and the second should clear it.

Use one ordinary state per independently held source when inputs can overlap. Combine those source states with an expression instead of writing several Hold mappings to the same destination.

docs.title: Pulse a state
docs.text:
1. Select Pulse.
  2. Under Pulse Options, set the pulse duration in milliseconds.
  3. Choose whether Pulse inverts state is enabled.
  4. Leave Pulse repeat off for the first test.
  5. Start the profile and observe the state through one complete pulse.

With Pulse inverts state enabled, the pulse toggles the state at its start and again at its end. This is useful when a pulse should temporarily invert an existing value. With it disabled, the pulse sets On and then Off. Avoid another mapping writing that state during the pulse when the original value matters.

New actions use a pulse duration of 250 ms, Pulse inverts state enabled, and repetition disabled. Pulse repeat adds repeated cycles with a separate repeat-delay field, also initially 250 ms. Test the full source press/release cycle and any profile mode change before using repeated pulses in a larger mapping.

Pulse duration and repeat delay are separate from the state's own Autorelease settings. Keep state-level Autorelease disabled for a simple action-controlled pulse.

docs.title: Latch a state for a fixed interval
docs.text:
Select Latch to turn an Off state On for Latch delay (ms). Repeated On requests during the active latch interval are ignored; they do not keep extending that interval. The state returns Off when the timer expires, and clearing it earlier ends the active latch.

  1. Select an ordinary Off state.
  2. Choose Latch and enter a positive delay, such as 1000 ms.
  3. Use press-only execution.
  4. Trigger it repeatedly during the first second, then wait for Off.

Use the State Editor's Autorelease controls when the timer rule should belong to the state itself. Use Latch when this mapping should initiate the timed On interval.

docs.title: Choose the triggering event
docs.text:
Use Execute on press for operations such as Press (on), Release (off), Toggle, or Latch when the command should run as a button is pressed. Use Execute on release when it should run as the source is released.

Enabling both can apply a one-shot operation twice during one physical press/release cycle. In particular, Toggle can turn On at the press and Off at the release.

Hold follows both values of the source. Pulse has its own cycle, so test it as a complete operation rather than using the trigger checkboxes as a pulse-duration control. Other State Mode uses the selected trigger events separately from the main operation.

docs.title: Apply an operation to other states
docs.text:
Other State Mode performs an additional operation on states outside the main target selection. Leave it on NoOp when only the selected targets should change.

To clear peers after selecting a state:

  1. Put the related ordinary states in one category.
  2. Choose the selected state's main operation, such as Press (on).
  3. Set Other State Mode to Release (off).
  4. Enable Category Only.
  5. Test each selection while watching all states in that category.

Category Only limits the additional operation to categories represented by the main targets. With it disabled, the additional operation reaches the profile's other states across categories. For a multi-target selection, the main targets are excluded from the additional operation.

Other State Mode also offers Press (on), Toggle, XOR, AND, and OR. For the Boolean operations, each target's value after the main operation is combined with each other state's current value:

  • XOR sets the other state On when its value differs from the target's value.
  • AND keeps the other state On only when both values are On.
  • OR sets the other state On when either value is On.

With several main targets, these combinations are applied successively for each target. Begin with a single target and a small category when configuring them.

Select main Mode NoOp when only the Other State Mode operation is needed. The main targets are still used to identify the excluded states, categories, and Boolean values.

For a group-wide selection rule that should apply whenever any mapping sets a member On, configure Mutually exclusive in the State Editor. Other State Mode is an operation attached to this particular action.

docs.title: Map a hat to states
docs.text:
On a raw hat input, assign states in the direction table rather than using the single button-mode selector:

  1. Add Map to State to the hat input.
  2. Select a state for each direction you need, including diagonals where appropriate.
  3. Choose Hold, Pulse, Press, Release, or NoOp for each position.
  4. Leave center unmapped or use NoOp unless centering should issue a command.
  5. Test each direction, adjacent transitions, diagonals, and return to center.

Use All Hold, All Pulse, All Press, All Release, or All NoOp to set the table's operation across positions. Clear Buttons clears its assignments; assign the required state names manually afterward.

When Apply to selects more than a single state, a position can also affect the additional selected targets. Test with State (single) and one mapped direction before adding a broader target selection.

docs.title: Use randomized state changes
docs.text:
Enable Randomize when an input should produce probabilistic state changes, such as a varied sequence or wiggle setup. The panel exposes Skip Chance % for adjusting the gate, and Pulse uses its own timing controls instead.

Keep Randomize off for switch tracking, bank selection, and command-enable states that must respond to every input. For a randomized setup, use a dedicated test state and watch many triggers in the viewer while adjusting the percentage. Add the randomized state to the final mapping after the observed result matches the intended use.

docs.title: Startup and stop settings
docs.text:
Use State on profile start to select initialization for the targets:

  • Ignore leaves this action out of startup synchronization. The State Device still applies the state's default initialization.
  • Default applies each target's Default State.
  • Input reads the source position. Use it with Hold for a maintained joystick switch; Invert reverses the sampled input.
  • LastOrInput requests the retained last value, using the source when no last value is available.
  • LastOrDefault requests the retained last value, using the configured default when none is available.

For a predictable switch setup, begin with Hold and Input. Test startup with the switch both On and Off, particularly when other actions also target the same state. Check the hat directions as well when synchronizing a raw hat mapping.

Reset to Default on stop returns the action's targets to their configured defaults when the profile stops. It is enabled for new actions. Save the profile after changing these choices; runtime On/Off values are separate from the saved state definitions.

docs.title: Track a panel switch
docs.text:
1. Create panel_power with Default State Off.
  2. Add Map to State to the switch input.
  3. Select panel_power, choose Hold, and set State on profile start to Input.
  4. Leave Other State Mode on NoOp and Randomize off.
  5. Start with the switch Off, then repeat the test with it already On.

Use panel_power in a condition or State container to enable the panel's commands.

docs.title: Trigger one state from another
docs.text:
Use one state as the input that changes a second state. In this example, a physical button holds light_request On, and each transition of light_request to On toggles aux_lights.

  1. In the State Device, create two ordinary states, light_request and aux_lights, both with Default State Off. Leave Autorelease and Mutually exclusive disabled.
  2. On a physical button, add Map to State. Select State (single), target light_request, and choose Hold.
  3. In the State Device tab, select light_request and add a Basic container to that state's mapping.
  4. Inside that container, add a second Map to State action. Set its target to aux_lights, choose Toggle, enable Execute on press, and disable Execute on release.
  5. Leave Other State Mode on NoOp and Randomize off on both actions. Use State on profile start: Ignore for this test.
  6. Save and start the profile. Display both states in the input viewer.
  7. Press the physical button. Light_request turns On, and its mapped action toggles aux_lights On.
  8. Release the physical button. Light_request turns Off; aux_lights stays On because its Toggle action executes only on the source state's press.
  9. Press again. Light_request turns On again and toggles aux_lights Off. Release to return light_request to Off.

The second Map to State action belongs to light_request's State Device mapping, with aux_lights selected as its target. This placement makes the state transition trigger the next action in the chain.

To observe a virtual output too, select aux_lights in the State Device and add a normal Hold-style Map to vJoy button action. The virtual button follows aux_lights and stays pressed between the first and second requests.

For a second state that should follow light_request On and Off instead of toggling independently, change the second Map to State action to Hold. Keep the chain directed from light_request to aux_lights; do not add a return mapping that changes light_request from aux_lights.

docs.title: Use a state as a condition
docs.text:
Use an enabling state to decide whether another input may set a command state. Here, commands_enabled gates a second button that holds command_active On.

  1. Create two ordinary states, commands_enabled and command_active, both with Default State Off.
  2. Map an enable button to commands_enabled using Toggle and execution on press only.
  3. On a separate command button, add a Basic container with Map to State targeting command_active. Choose Hold, Other State Mode NoOp, and Randomize off.
  4. Open the conditions for that Map to State action and add a State condition.
  5. Select commands_enabled, choose Pressed to require On, and enable Apply condition on press only so the command's release can still pass through.
  6. Save and start the profile, then watch both states in the input viewer.
  7. With commands_enabled Off, press and release the command button. Command_active remains Off.
  8. Press the enable button to turn commands_enabled On. Hold the command button: command_active turns On. Release it: command_active turns Off.
  9. Test release handling by holding the command button, turning commands_enabled Off with the enable button, and then releasing the command button. Command_active must return Off.

Changing commands_enabled alone does not press command_active. The condition is checked when the command button's event arrives. The state-triggered mapping in the previous example is the setup to use when a state transition should initiate another action directly.

You can place the same condition on another action, such as a virtual button or keyboard mapping, or select an expression state when several requirements must be met. See the State Device condition example for a compound condition.

docs.title: Toggle an alternate command layer
docs.text:
1. Create alternate_layer with Default State Off.
  2. Map the layer button to it using Toggle and execution on press only.
  3. Put alternate commands in State containers requiring alternate_layer On/Pressed.
  4. Put ordinary commands in containers requiring alternate_layer Off/Released.
  5. Test switching layers with all command buttons released, then test the release handling needed by any held outputs.

docs.title: Clear a group of flags
docs.text:
1. Add the attribute reset_on_command to the ordinary states that should be cleared together.
  2. Add Map to State to the reset button and choose Apply to: Attributes.
  3. Pick reset_on_command and inspect the matched names.
  4. Choose Release (off), press-only execution, Other State Mode NoOp, and Randomize off.
  5. Turn several flags On in the viewer and press reset.

Use Category instead when every ordinary state in one or more complete categories should be cleared.

docs.title: Select one state in a category
docs.text:
1. Create radio_1, radio_2, and radio_3 in a radios category.
  2. Map each selection button to its own state using Press (on).
  3. On each action, choose Other State Mode Release (off) and enable Category Only.
  4. Use press-only execution.
  5. Test that selecting one radio clears its peers while states in other categories remain as configured.

Use the State Editor's Mutually exclusive group instead when every writer of these states should apply the same peer-clearing rule.

docs.title: Test the mapping
docs.text:
Use the input viewer to inspect the target values before binding their outputs in a game:

  1. Check the source event and the main target selection.
  2. Test press and release separately.
  3. For Category or Attributes, inspect every matched state.
  4. Check any additional Other State Mode targets.
  5. Observe dependent expression states and their output mappings.
  6. Repeat from a fresh profile start with the hardware in different positions.

If the result is unclear, reduce the setup to one ordinary state, one physical button, Hold or Toggle, Other State Mode NoOp, and Randomize off. Add expressions, group operations, and timers after that mapping works.

docs.title: Map to vJoy — User Guide
docs.text:
Map to vJoy sends an input to a virtual joystick output. It supports vJoy and HIDMaestro output devices. Use it to map a physical control to a virtual axis, button, or hat; turn an axis range into a button; combine axes; or move an axis with buttons or an encoder.

The action supersedes the legacy remap action.

The action is also identified as Vjoy Remap and Map to Vjoy. This guide describes the supplied GremlinEx implementation. Available controls depend on the source input and the selected action mode. Mode descriptions below describe their behavior; the wording in the Mode list may vary by build.

docs.text:
