docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Have the following ready:

  • A GremlinEx profile containing the source input you want to use.
  • A connected virtual output device with the axis, button, or hat you need.
  • A way to observe the virtual output while testing, such as the application's output display or a joystick monitor.

Configure the target game or application to use the virtual output you select. A physical input and its virtual output are separate controls; verify which one the target application has bound.

For the first test, use one source input and one virtual output. Add curves, merging, or remote output after the basic mapping works.

You can test output values in the GEX input viewer. For vJoy devices, you can also use the vJoy Monitor utility included with your vJoy installation. For HIDMaestro, use a joystick monitor on the computer hosting the controller. This is often faster and easier than testing in the game directly.

docs.title: Choose a virtual output device
docs.text:
The Device list includes available vJoy devices and HIDMaestro devices included in GremlinEx. Select the device by name, then choose an output that it actually exposes. Devices with different axis, button, or hat counts offer different output choices.

For vJoy, configure and enable the virtual controller with your vJoy installation before selecting it in the action.

For HIDMaestro:

  1. Run the Maestro Bridge service on the computer that will host the virtual controller.
  2. Enable the Maestro module in GremlinEx's module configuration if needed.
  3. Open Tools → Maestro Devices... and enter the service Host and Port, plus the local reply address and Reply port. The reply port must match the service's SendPort.
  4. Use Refresh Devices to load the host's devices. Select an existing device, or create one with New Device or Presets....
  5. Ensure the device is Active on host, check Include in Gremlin, and select Apply to Gremlin.
  6. Select that controller in the action's Device list, choose the output, and test it.

Maestro output uses the configured bridge connection, including when the bridge runs on another computer. The virtual controller is available to games on the host computer. The action's separate remote-vJoy routing controls do not select the Maestro host; see Local and remote output.

docs.title: Axis values
docs.text:
Axis settings generally use a normalized range:

Value Meaning -1.0 Low end 0.0 Center +1.0 High end

The full span is 2.0 units. A change of 0.05 is 2.5% of the full span. Center does not necessarily mean “off” in a game; that depends on the control you bind.

docs.title: Create your first mapping
docs.text:
1. Select the profile mode and source input you want to map.
  2. Add Map to vJoy to the input's action container.
  3. In Mode, select the required mapping behavior. For a simple test, use direct axis, button, or hat mapping to match the source control.
  4. In Device, select the destination virtual joystick.
  5. In Output, select its axis, button, or hat.
  6. Save the profile and start it.
  7. Operate the source control and observe the virtual output.
  8. Bind that virtual output in the target game or application.

Next Unused selects an available output according to the profile's usage information. It does not guarantee that the output is unused by other applications.

Show disconnected includes unavailable virtual devices in the selector. Selecting one does not connect it. Resolve the device warning before relying on the mapping.

docs.title: Choose a mapping mode
docs.text:
The Mode list changes with the input type. Select the source input first, then choose the behavior.

Source Available behavior families Axis Direct axis output, axis-to-button, axis merging Button or input treated as a button Button hold/invert/press/release/pulse/toggle; hat output; axis inversion; set-axis; stepped-axis; change-axis-range; merging; local/remote control commands Hat Direct hat output or hat-to-button mapping

Keyboard and other supported event inputs may be treated as buttons by the surrounding input/container configuration. Use Override input type only when the action needs to interpret an input as an axis, button, or hat differently from its current configuration. An override changes the interpretation; it does not create missing input data.

docs.title: Absolute axis mapping
docs.text:
Use Absolute when the virtual axis should follow the source axis position.

  1. Choose the axis mapping mode.
  2. Select the destination device and axis.
  3. Select Absolute.
  4. Move the source through its full travel.
  5. Enable Reverse Axis if the direction is opposite to the one you need.

For example, a throttle can drive a virtual throttle axis directly, while a stick axis can drive virtual pitch or roll.

docs.title: Limit the output range
docs.text:
Under Output Scale, set Range Min and Range Max to constrain the output span.

Range Min Range Max Resulting span -1.0 +1.0 Full travel -0.5 +0.5 Middle half of full travel 0.0 +1.0 Upper half of the normalized range

Use Reset to restore the normal full range. Test both endpoints after changing the range.

docs.title: Apply an output curve
docs.text:
Select Output Curve to edit the action's curve. A curve changes how input movement translates into output movement—for example, to make movement near the center less sensitive.

Use the adjacent remove control to clear the action's output curve. Other curves applied elsewhere in the input configuration can still affect the result. Watch the input/output values rather than assuming this is the only curve in the profile.

docs.title: Relative axis mapping
docs.text:
Use Relative when the source should increase or decrease the current output instead of commanding an absolute position.

  1. Select Relative.
  2. Set Relative Value, the amount applied per update.
  3. Set the pulse/update delay in milliseconds.
  4. For a centered analog input, enable Use relative value so the amount is scaled by input deflection and updates stop near the center.
  5. Test movement in both directions and return the source to center.

Smaller increments or longer delays produce slower movement. Reversing the axis reverses the direction of relative adjustment.

Unlike Absolute mode, returning the source to center normally leaves the virtual axis at its accumulated position. Verify the stop behavior before using a large increment.

docs.title: Map buttons
docs.text:
Choose the behavior that matches the desired output state.

Behavior What it does Typical use Hold / normal button Output follows the input's pressed/released state. Momentary commands Inverted button Output uses the opposite input state. Reversing switch logic Press Sets the output button on without automatically pairing it with a release. One input turns a function on Release Sets the output button off. A second input turns that function off Pulse Sends a timed press followed by a release. A brief command from a switch or button Toggle Alternates the output state on successive qualifying triggers. Latching a function with one button

For a normal momentary mapping, start with Hold and leave Ignore release off. For Press mappings, provide a deliberate way to release the same output, such as a separate Release action.

docs.title: Trigger on press or release
docs.text:
The execution controls select whether supported actions run on the source press, release, or both. They are especially useful for pulse, set-axis, and command actions.

Select only the event you need for a one-shot action. Enabling both can cause one physical press-and-release cycle to trigger the action twice. Hold-style mappings still need the appropriate release behavior to avoid leaving the output on.

docs.title: Pulse timing
docs.text:
• Pulse Delay is the duration of the output press, in milliseconds.
  • Repeat delay controls the spacing of repeated pulses.
  • Enable pulse repetition to keep pulsing while the triggering condition remains active.

The supplied default duration is 125 ms; the default repeat delay is also 125 ms. If the target application misses brief pulses, increase the duration and test again.

docs.title: Turn an axis range into a button
docs.text:
Use axis-to-button mapping for a detent, end-stop, or position zone.

  1. Select the source axis and add the action.
  2. Choose the axis-to-button mode.
  3. Select a destination device and button.
  4. Set Axis to Button Range Min and Range Max.
  5. Choose Hold or Pulse.
  6. Move into, within, and out of the range while observing the output.

Use the grab controls to capture the current axis value as either boundary.

Quick setting Range Reset -1.0 to +1.0 Half -0.5 to +0.5 L-Half -1.0 to 0.0 U-Half 0.0 to +1.0 Bot -1.0 to -0.75 Top +0.75 to +1.0

Hold keeps the output on while the axis is in range and releases it when the axis leaves. Pulse starts when the axis enters the range; repetition, if enabled, continues until it leaves.

For a throttle detent near the high end, try 0.90 to 1.00. These are example values; use the displayed axis value to find the correct range for your device. Curves and other axis processing can affect the value being tested.

For position-dependent behavior, use Hold or Pulse in this version. See Behavior notes for this version before using the range panel's Press or Release options.

docs.title: Hat to virtual hat
docs.text: Select the hat mapping mode, destination device, and output hat. Test all eight directions and the centered position.

docs.title: Button to hat
docs.text:
For button-based hat output, select the output hat and configure:

  • Press Position: the direction to send when activated.
  • Release position: the position to send when released or when a pulse completes.

Choose centered as the release position when the hat should return to neutral. Use a hat press action to retain a position, or a hat pulse action for a timed direction command.

docs.title: Hat to buttons
docs.text:
Use hat-to-button mapping when the target application needs separate buttons for hat positions.

  1. Choose the hat-to-button mode and destination device.
  2. Assign a button to each direction you want to use.
  3. Choose a behavior for each position.
  4. Configure the center position deliberately; select Not mapped or NoOp if it should not issue a command.
  5. Test transitions between adjacent directions, diagonals, and center.
Per-position behavior Result Hold Tracks the active position and releases previously held positions as the hat changes. Pulse Sends a timed output for that position. Press Turns the selected button on. Release Turns the selected button off. NoOp Sends no output for that position.

Map Buttons assigns sequential button numbers, using the first position's selection as a starting reference when set. Clear Buttons removes the assignments. The All Hold, All Pulse, All Press, All Release, and All NoOp controls set the behavior across the table.

After automatic assignment, check every row, including center. Stay within the destination device's available button count. NoOp means “do nothing”; it should not be used as an implicit release command for an output you intentionally left on.

docs.title: Set an axis with a button
docs.text:
Choose the set-axis mode when a button should command a particular virtual axis position.

  1. Select a button-like input.
  2. Choose set-axis mode and the destination axis.
  3. Enter Set Value within -1.0 to +1.0.
  4. Select the triggering event, usually press only.
  5. Start the profile and test the button.

Examples include setting a throttle to an idle position or centering a virtual control at 0.0.

Is Relative is presented as the option for adding the entered value to the current output. In the supplied implementation, that checkbox does not control the setting read by the set-axis output routine, so do not rely on it alone for incremental movement. For repeatable increments, use the stepped-axis modes below. Axis output is limited to the normalized bounds.

Use last resends the last axis value with a small temporary movement intended to make the target application reread it. Use it only when that behavior is needed.

Two related modes are available for button-like inputs:

  • Invert axis changes the target axis's reversal state when triggered.
  • Change axis range changes the range used for the selected output axis. It does not itself move a physical input.

docs.title: Control an axis with two inputs
docs.text:
Choose the stepped-axis action mode, then select a behavior under Button to Axis (step) Mode:

Mode How the axis moves Typical use Velocity Moves continuously while the input is held. Hold a button to adjust trim. Stepped Jumps directly to the next configured preset. Discrete flap positions. Stepped+PID Moves smoothly toward the next configured preset. Flaps that travel gradually between detents. Encoder Accumulates pulses, with optional speed-based acceleration or return to center. Rotary encoder adjustment. PID Changes a target by a configured amount and follows it smoothly. Fine trim adjustment with momentary inputs.

All five modes share Initial axis value and the secondary reverse-input configuration. See Set the startup position for fixed and automatic initialization.

docs.title: Set the reverse input
docs.text:
The source input is the primary control. To add a control for the opposite direction:

  1. Enable Latch secondary input for reverse action.
  2. Under Latched Input Type, choose Keyboard or Joystick.
  3. For Keyboard, use Select Keys to define the secondary key sequence.
  4. For Joystick, select the device and input, or use the listen control. Select the direction when using a hat input.
  5. Test each input separately.

Here, “secondary” or “latched” input is a reverse-direction trigger. It is not an instruction to hold the primary and secondary controls together. A keyboard sequence assigned to the secondary trigger can itself require multiple simultaneous keys.

Use a distinct control or key combination for each direction. Begin with execution on press only and test both controls, including their releases. See Behavior notes for this version for the current direction-selector limitation in Stepped, Stepped+PID, and PID modes.

docs.title: Set the startup position
docs.text:
For a fixed startup position, choose a numbered step preset so Initial axis value is editable, then enter a value or move its slider. The configured value is sent immediately when the profile starts; the mode's movement state starts from the same position. Even Stepped+PID and PID initialize immediately rather than easing from the previous output.

In Stepped and Stepped+PID, Use step preset: Start Index and the selection beside an individual step copy that preset into Initial axis value. The start index is numbered from 1. The slider shows the configured step positions as tick marks, and Preset value shows the selected preset.

Auto requests initialization from the current virtual output axis position instead of the configured initial value. It reads the virtual output, not the physical source control. When Auto is active, the fixed startup controls are disabled. The current editor has an Auto-selection limitation; check Behavior notes for this version before relying on it.

docs.title: Velocity: move while held
docs.text:
Use Velocity for continuous adjustment while a button is held.

Setting Effect Update Interval (ms) Time between output updates. Rate of change Axis movement per second. Acceleration How quickly the movement rate changes; 0 gives a constant rate.

Choose a modest rate, test a short press, and then test a longer hold. The secondary input moves in the opposite direction.

docs.title: Stepped: move between presets
docs.text:
Use Stepped for a fixed set of positions, such as flap or mixture presets.

  1. Define the step values, keeping them in ascending order within -1.0 to +1.0.
  2. Adjust Steps, use Add Step, edit the comma-separated list or individual values, or choose a list from Presets.... Use the delete control beside a value to remove it.
  3. Check Step direction and test which input increases or decreases the output; see the current direction-selector limitation.
  4. Choose Use step preset: Start Index or select an individual step to set the startup value. Verify Preset value and Initial axis value.
  5. Start the profile and test each direction from the configured startup position.

Presets... replaces the step list with a supplied distribution, including evenly spaced lists, Ends + Quarters + Center (9), and geometric low/high lists. Review the resulting values and count before running the profile.

Distribution controls help generate values:

Control Purpose Normalize Even spacing Low / High More positions toward the low or high portion of the range Geometric Low / Geometric High Nonlinear spacing toward an end Cubic Center Cubic progression around the center

The step sequence stops at its endpoints rather than wrapping. Keep the list nonempty and verify the first trigger in each direction, especially if Initial axis value lies between presets.

docs.title: Stepped+PID: move smoothly between presets
docs.text:
Use Stepped+PID when you want the same discrete target positions as Stepped, with gradual movement between them.

  1. Select Stepped+PID under Button to Axis (step) Mode.
  2. Define the step values with the same preset, list-editing, and distribution controls used by Stepped.
  3. Select a startup preset and check Initial axis value.
  4. Configure the secondary reverse input and use execution on press only for the first test.
  5. Start the profile and observe the output during single presses, rapid presses, and a direction change.

Each trigger requests the next preset. The axis moves faster at first and eases into that target, continuing after the button is released. Further triggers choose presets from the commanded target while the output is still moving. For example, with presets -1.0, -0.5, 0.0, 0.5, and 1.0, two increase triggers from 0.0 request 0.5 and then 1.0 without waiting for the first transition to finish. The sequence stops at its endpoints.

Stepped+PID uses the exact preset values as targets. PID's Setpoint change per press and faster-input acceleration do not enlarge these preset steps. The current Stepped+PID panel shows the stepped controls; response-time editing and saving have a limitation described in Behavior notes for this version.

docs.title: Encoder: adjust with pulses
docs.text:
Use Encoder when a rotary control generates momentary events in each direction.

Bind one direction as the primary input and the other as the secondary reverse input. Then choose:

Setting Effect Relative Keeps the accumulated axis position after rotation stops. Spring Returns the axis to center after pulses stop. Spring delay (ms) Idle time before the return to center. Min Step / Max Step Smallest and largest movement per pulse. Start Frequency (Hz) Pulse frequency where acceleration begins. Full Frequency (Hz) Pulse frequency that reaches the maximum step. Curve Power Shapes how the step grows with input speed. Timeout (ms) Idle time before acceleration resets.

Keep Full Frequency above Start Frequency. Use small steps for fine adjustment and larger accelerated steps for rapid travel. In Spring mode, use a positive spring delay if automatic return is required.

docs.title: PID: move a target and follow it smoothly
docs.text:
Use PID when each momentary press should change a target position and the axis should move smoothly toward it. The axis moves quickly at first and eases into the target.

  1. Select PID.
  2. Set Initial axis value.
  3. Set Setpoint change per press.
  4. Set Response time (s).
  5. Assign the increase control as primary and the decrease control as secondary; see the current direction-selector limitation.
  6. Configure the secondary reverse input if needed.
  7. Test single presses before enabling acceleration.
Setting Supplied default Meaning Setpoint change per press 0.05 Change in the target per incoming press event. Response time (s) 1.0 Approximate time to close 99% of the gap; lower values make the response faster.

With execution on press only, PID changes the target on incoming press events; it continues following the target after release. If the input source produces repeated press events while held, those events can produce additional target changes. Use Velocity for continuous movement while held. Additional qualifying triggers adjust the commanded target while the axis is still moving, and an opposite trigger can redirect it before it settles.

Response time (s) accepts 0.05 to 120.0 seconds. It scales the whole curved transition; it is not a constant movement speed or an exact arrival deadline. Use Stepped+PID when targets must come from a fixed list of presets.

Enable Accelerate setpoint steps with faster input to make rapid presses change the target by larger amounts.

Acceleration setting Supplied default Meaning Maximum step multiplier 4.0 Largest step relative to the base step. Acceleration starts (triggers/s) 2.0 At or below this rate, use the base step. Full acceleration (triggers/s) 12.0 Rate that reaches the maximum step. Acceleration curve 2.0 Higher values delay the increase toward the maximum step. Idle reset (s) 0.75 A pause this long resets acceleration; direction changes reset it too.

Keep Full acceleration above Acceleration starts. Output remains within -1.0 to +1.0.

docs.title: Merge axes
docs.text:
Use axis merging to combine a primary axis with one or more additional axes.

  1. Select the primary axis and choose the merge-axis mode.
  2. Choose the destination device and axis.
  3. In Merge Information, select a Merge Device and Merge Axis, or use the listen control.
  4. Choose the merge operation.
  5. Configure a curve for the additional axis if needed.
  6. Test each source separately, then move them together.
  7. Add further merge entries only after the first combination behaves correctly.

Each merge entry uses the running result as A and its selected axis as B. Entries are processed in order, so changing the sequence can change the result.

Operation family Use Add Combines A and B by addition. Average Uses (A + B) / 2. Center Uses (A - B) / 2, useful for opposing controls. Minimum / Maximum Chooses the lower or higher value. Multiply Uses one input to scale the other by multiplication. Scale variants Uses B as a scaling control; centered and half variants interpret B differently. Trim / Trim (centered) Uses B to adjust the primary axis's response.

Scaling and range processing also affect the final output. For scale and trim variants, watch the live values while moving B through both ends and center rather than assuming the variant matches your device's rest position.

Use Reverse Axis to invert the primary input before merging. Use Invert Merged Output to reverse the final combined result.

When axis repeaters are enabled, each merge entry shows a Step Output value for its selected source axis. The main Output preview reflects the combined result and updates when either the primary axis or an additional merge axis moves. Use both displays to check which input changes the result before testing in the target application.

docs.title: Startup state
docs.text:
Where displayed, the startup synchronization controls let you initialize an output from a configured default or the source input. Test startup with the source in more than one position to confirm that the initial output is appropriate.

The five button-to-axis modes initialize separately from the general synchronization controls: they apply Initial axis value, or reuse the virtual output position when Auto is active. See Set the startup position.

docs.title: Local and remote output
docs.text:
For vJoy destinations, the action includes output routing through its remote-client controls. Check the routing when a mapping works remotely but not locally, or vice versa.

Button-like inputs can also select command modes that enable or disable local output, enable or disable remote output, choose local-only or remote-only output, enable both, toggle remote output, or control paired remote behavior. These commands change routing state; they are not ordinary button mappings.

Configure remote clients through the application's remote-output features before using remote routing. Leave Paired Group Member unchanged unless the mapping is part of an intentionally paired setup.

For HIDMaestro destinations, axis, button, and hat output goes through the configured Maestro Bridge connection. Remote-vJoy client selection and local/remote-vJoy switches do not redirect that output. Change the host in Tools → Maestro Devices... when the controller is provided by a different Maestro service.

docs.title: Release and display options
docs.text: Option Use Ignore release Suppresses release handling where supported. Normally leave it off for a momentary mapping. Auto Release Requests release handling for inputs/containers that need it. Test the entire press/release cycle. Show button grid Shows the output assignment grid. Override input type Changes how the action interprets the source input.

docs.title: A throttle with a high-end detent button
docs.text:
Create two actions on the throttle input:

  1. A direct Absolute mapping to the virtual throttle axis.
  2. An axis-to-button mapping to a separate virtual button, using a range of 0.90 to 1.00 and Hold behavior.

The virtual axis follows the throttle. The virtual button turns on near the high end and off when the throttle leaves the zone. Adjust the boundary using the live value on your hardware.

docs.title: Five discrete flap positions
docs.text:
1. Add the stepped-axis action to the increase control.
  2. Select Stepped and the virtual flap axis.
  3. Choose Presets... → 5 steps, giving -1.0, -0.5, 0.0, 0.5, and 1.0.
  4. Set Use step preset: Start Index to 1 and verify that Initial axis value is -1.0.
  5. Configure a secondary reverse control.
  6. Start the profile and verify that each trigger moves to the adjacent preset and stops at the ends.

docs.title: Smooth flap transitions
docs.text:
1. Configure the five flap presets from the previous example.
  2. Change the mode from Stepped to Stepped+PID.
  3. Verify Initial axis value and the secondary reverse control.
  4. Start the profile and press the increase control once. The output should travel smoothly toward -0.5.
  5. Press again during that movement to request 0.0, then test the reverse control while the axis is moving.

The target positions remain the configured detents, while the virtual axis travels through intermediate values. Bind this output to a game control that accepts an axis. Reload the saved profile and retest the transition timing; see the Stepped+PID settings limitation.

docs.title: Smooth trim adjustment
docs.text:
1. Add the stepped-axis action to the trim-increase control.
  2. Select PID and the virtual trim axis.
  3. Set Initial axis value to 0.0, Setpoint change per press to 0.02, and Response time (s) to 0.5.
  4. Select Primary increases and assign trim-decrease as the secondary input.
  5. Leave acceleration off for the initial test.

Each press moves the target by 0.02; the virtual axis follows smoothly. These are example settings, not the supplied defaults.

docs.title: One hat, separate command buttons
docs.text:
1. Select the physical hat and choose hat-to-button mapping.
  2. Assign a different virtual button to each direction you need.
  3. Use Hold for commands that should remain active while held, or Pulse for brief commands.
  4. Leave unused directions unassigned and configure center deliberately.
  5. Test transitions through diagonals before binding the buttons in the target application.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom Check No virtual output Profile running; correct profile mode; action/container enabled; destination connected; valid output selected; local/remote routing. Virtual output works, but the game does not respond The game is bound to the selected virtual device and output rather than the physical control or another virtual device. Desired axis, button, or hat is missing The selected destination actually exposes that output type and number. Output moves backward Reverse Axis, final merge inversion, and other curves or reversal settings. Axis does not reach the expected endpoints Output Scale, output curves, merge operations, and any range-changing action on that output. Relative axis keeps moving at center Enable Use relative value for deflection-scaled updates; verify the source returns near zero. Button remains on Press/toggle behavior, Ignore release, missing Release action, or a container that does not deliver release events. One press causes two adjustments Both press and release selected, duplicate actions targeting the output, or repeated input events. Pulses are missed Increase pulse duration; verify the destination button and trigger condition. Axis-range button activates at the wrong position Observe the processed axis value, review the range, and check the behavior notes below. Secondary input does nothing Enable reverse-input latching; verify Keyboard/Joystick selection, device, input, hat direction, and relevant conditions. Stepped axis starts at an unexpected value Check Initial axis value, the selected Start Index, and whether Auto is active. Preset selection now copies the preset into Initial axis value. Stepped axis stops changing It may have reached the first or last preset. Stepped+PID jumps immediately on profile start Expected for a fixed startup value. Smoothing applies to subsequent target changes. Stepped+PID timing changes after reloading The current profile writer does not save its PID response-time setting; see the behavior notes below. PID output continues after release Expected: it is finishing the move to the target. Increase/decrease Response time to change the transition speed. Direction selector does not reverse PID or preset stepping The current handlers use primary for increase and secondary for decrease; swap the assigned controls and see the behavior notes below. Encoder feels too fast or too slow Min Step, Max Step, acceleration frequencies, Curve Power, and Timeout. Merged axis jumps or disagrees with expectations Source rest positions, curves, operation order, conflicting writers to the same output, and final inversion. Maestro device is missing from Device Maestro module enabled; bridge running; correct host, service port, and reply settings; device active on host and included in Gremlin; Apply to Gremlin completed. Maestro output goes to the wrong computer Check the Maestro Bridge host. Remote-vJoy routing does not choose the Maestro host.

When diagnosing a problem, temporarily reduce the mapping to one action with no extra curve or merge. Verify the input event, the virtual output, and then the target application's binding in that order.

docs.title: Play Sound — User Guide
docs.text:
Play Sound/TTS plays an audio file or generates speech from text and plays the resulting audio. Use it for button feedback, spoken status messages, alternate announcements, or a repeating sound cue. The documentation also refers to this action as Play Sound.

The current action offers Audio file, TTS (local), AI (Edge-TTS), and Stop Playback modes. Playback uses a shared audio queue, with options for device selection, overlap, repetition, fades, silence trimming, and duplicate suppression.

docs.title: Contents
docs.text:
• Play Sound — User Guide
  • Contents

  • Create your first sound mapping
  • Choose a source mode
    • Audio file
    • TTS (local)
    • AI (Edge-TTS)

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Have a profile containing the source input and an available audio output device. For Audio file mode, start with a short, known-good WAV file. The file picker also accepts MP3; WAV avoids a compressed-file decoding step and is a useful first test when playback fails or starts slowly.

The action declares support for joystick buttons and hats. Hat inputs need virtual-button activation directions so the action receives a pressed/released state. Other input types depend on the surrounding input configuration; do not assume the action can be added directly to every raw axis.

For an initial test, use one button, one WAV file, one playback loop, and execution on press only. Leave maximum playback duration and fades at 0, and keep Stop previous audio and Block playback off.

docs.title: Create your first sound mapping
docs.text:
1. Select the profile mode and source input.
  2. Add Play Sound/TTS to the input's action container.
  3. Select Audio file.
  4. Use the folder control beside Sound file to select a WAV file.
  5. Enable Use system default playback device, or select a specific output as described below.
  6. Set Volume to a comfortable level and Loops to 1.
  7. Use the play control to preview the configured audio. Its tooltip is Generate & Play in the speech controls.
  8. Enable Execute on press and disable Execute on release.
  9. Save and start the profile, then press the source button.

The preview tests the sound configuration. Runtime playback also depends on the active profile mode, enabled actions, and container/action conditions.

docs.title: Choose a source mode
docs.text: Mode Source Main requirement Audio file An existing WAV or MP3 file. The file remains accessible on disk. TTS (local) Text generated using an installed operating-system voice. A working local voice; no online synthesis service is used. AI (Edge-TTS) Text generated through Edge-TTS, then converted to WAV. A connection for new speech generation and a working FFmpeg conversion. Stop Playback Stops shared playback and clears pending audio. No audio file. Saving/reloading this mode has a current limitation; see the behavior notes.

docs.title: Audio file
docs.text:
Select an actual audio file in Sound file, rather than a directory. You can type a path or browse for one. The adjacent delete control clears the action's file selection; it does not delete that source file from disk. The default file format is .WAV to minimize overhead and reduce playback latency.

The profile stores the file path, not an embedded copy of the audio. If you move or share the profile, make the referenced files available on the destination computer and update their paths where needed.

Enable Randomize from folder to choose samples from the selected file's containing folder. See Samples from a folder for its selection behavior.

docs.title: TTS (local)
docs.text:
1. Select TTS (local).
  2. Enter the announcement in Text.
  3. Choose a Voice under pytts Generation Options. Use the refresh control if the available voice list has changed.
  4. Set Rate (wpm). New actions use 100; the editor accepts 50 to 300 words per minute.
  5. Select Generate, then use the play control to preview the result.

This mode generates a reusable WAV file using the local speech engine. The voices depend on what is installed on the computer. Change the main Volume control to adjust how loudly the generated sample plays; generation-volume controls have a limitation described in the behavior notes. This mode is provided for legacy compatibility reasons and is not recommended. Please use the AI mode instead for high sound quality and rich voice options.

docs.title: AI (Edge-TTS)
docs.text:
1. Select AI (Edge-TTS).
  2. Enter the text.
  3. Under ETTS Generation Options, filter by Locale and Gender, then choose a Voice. Use refresh to update the voice list.
  4. Leave Rate% (gen) and Pitch Offset (Hz) at 0 for the first test.
  5. Select Generate, wait for the result, and preview it.

Rate% (gen) changes speech speed during generation: 0 is the normal rate, +100 requests twice the rate, and -50 requests half the rate. Pitch Offset (Hz) adjusts the generated voice pitch. These are generation settings, separate from playback volume and timing. Retest after saving and reopening the profile; pitch persistence has a current limitation.

New Edge-TTS synthesis uses a free cloud service. GremlinEx converts all audio to the .WAV file format and caches this data so generation only occurs once if the audio is not cached for the current playback parameters. This ensures that the cloud service is only used to generate audio once, and the audio is cross-profile, meaning that other profiles with the same TTS parameters will be shared between projects.

For an announcement that must work without new synthesis, export its generated WAV and use Audio file mode.

docs.title: Generate, cache, and save speech
docs.text:
Text, engine, voice, rate, pitch, and generation-volume settings identify a cached phrase. Reusing that phrase can reuse its generated audio. Changing those settings or the translated text can require generation again.

  • Generate forces regeneration of the configured phrases.
  • The play control generates missing audio as needed and previews the selected phrase with the playback settings.
  • The save control, with tooltip Save the audio file(s), exports generated WAV files. One phrase opens a file-save dialog; multiple phrases open a destination-folder dialog.
  • The status area reports the result and can offer a control to open the saved file's folder.

Generated audio is kept in GremlinEx's managed sounds repository, under sounds/managed in its user-profile folder, with a phrase index named phrases.xml. It is separate from the mapping profile. Saving the profile is not the same as exporting or transferring its generated audio.

The action attempts to prepare local and Edge-TTS audio at profile activation. The application also offers Generate TTS on load in its Voice (TTS) options; enabling it can increase profile load time when speech needs generating.

Auto Generate is shown for speech modes, but the current activation/playback paths can generate missing audio regardless of that checkbox. Generate and preview important phrases before starting the profile when predictable trigger timing matters.

docs.title: Use alternate phrases and folder samples
Alternate spoken phrases
docs.text:
Separate alternatives with vertical bars in Text, for example:

Gear down.|Landing gear extended.|Gear is down.

Each nonempty segment becomes a separate phrase. A trigger chooses one phrase; it does not speak the whole list. Newlines alone are not the phrase separator used by this action.

Multi mode selects how speech alternatives are chosen:

Multi mode Behavior Round Robin Cycles through the available phrases in order. Random Makes an independent random choice on each trigger. Immediate repeats are possible. Timed Random Prefers choices not used during the randomizer's cooldown. When all choices are in cooldown, it can reuse one.

Timed Random does not start a timer that speaks automatically. It still needs input triggers. The action creates its selection randomizer with a 10-second cooldown; this is separate from Suppress Duplicate Playback.

docs.title: Samples from a folder
docs.text:
In Audio file mode, enable Randomize from folder after selecting a sample in the desired folder. The scan includes WAV and MP3 entries in that folder and does not descend into subfolders. Restart the profile after changing the folder contents to refresh the runtime list.

Folder selection uses the action's timed randomizer, preferring recently unused files where possible. The Multi mode radio buttons control speech alternatives; they do not change the folder-selection algorithm in this version. A trigger chooses one file, then Loops repeats that chosen sample rather than choosing another file for each loop.

docs.title: Dynamic text
docs.text:
The action substitutes ${current_mode} with the active profile mode name before generating speech:

Current mode is ${current_mode}.

A mode name that has not been generated before can require a new cached phrase. Test the expected modes before relying on immediate speech output.

Text is also sanitized: parenthesized content and backtick-delimited text are removed, and characters outside Windows-1252 can be replaced. Preview announcements containing non-Latin text or special symbols. Use a prepared audio file when that processing would alter the required wording.

docs.title: Choose the playback device
docs.text:
Use system default playback device is enabled for new actions. It follows the Windows default output when playback is requested, which is useful when switching between speakers and a headset.

To use a fixed endpoint:

  1. Disable Use system default playback device.
  2. Choose the endpoint in Playback device.
  3. Preview the sound and confirm the correct device is audible.

The Default button selects the currently detected default endpoint. Use the checkbox when you want to keep following later Windows default-device changes. If a fixed endpoint cannot be found, playback can fall back to the default device; check the log and test again after reconnecting audio hardware.

Sync All copies the selected device setting to Play Sound actions throughout the profile. Control-clicking Default similarly applies the current default endpoint across the profile. These operations do not disable each action's follow-default checkbox, so review that checkbox on actions that must use a fixed device.

Different actions can target different endpoints. Concurrent sounds can also play through the same endpoint.

docs.title: Adjust volume, loops, fades, and trimming
docs.text:
Control New-action value Meaning Volume 100 Playback level from 0 to 100 percent. 0 is silent. Loops 1 Total number of sample plays, from 1 to 100. 1 means play once. Max playback (s) 0 Intended duration limit; 0 disables it. The current editor has a unit-conversion issue, so verify nonzero values before use. Fade-in (ms) 0 Ramp from silence at the start of the processed sample. 0 disables the fade. Fade-out (ms) 0 Ramp to silence at the end of the processed sample. 0 disables the fade. Silence Trim All Remove eligible silence at both ends of the sample. Threshold (dB) -55 Audio below this level is considered silence.

Fades are applied to the sample used for each loop. A fade longer than a short sample can affect its entire duration. These options process playback data; they do not rewrite the source audio file.

Silence Trim offers None, All, and End. None preserves the audio, All trims both ends, and End trims only trailing silence. Lower thresholds, such as -60 dB, preserve quieter material; a higher threshold can remove a quiet start or ending. If a sound disappears or loses part of a word, test with None and adjust the threshold.

The playback engine also supports a pitch-preserving playback-rate setting, separate from speech-generation rate. Its editor control is not currently placed in the visible layout; see the behavior notes rather than assuming a visible rate control is available.

docs.title: Choose when the action runs
docs.text:
Trigger selection Result Execute on press only Starts playback when the source becomes pressed. This is the default. Execute on release only Starts playback when the source is released. Both A physical press/release cycle can request playback twice. Neither Input events do not request playback.

Releasing the source does not normally stop a clip started on press. Loops controls a fixed repeat count, not repetition for as long as the source remains held. Use a suitable container for repeated triggering, and account for the shared queue and stop behavior below.

docs.title: Control overlapping and queued audio
docs.text:
By default, playback is asynchronous and accepted requests can overlap. Repeated triggers can play multiple instances of the same sample, and the profile continues processing other mappings.

Option Effect Stop previous audio Stops active shared audio before this queued sample starts. It can interrupt sounds started by other Play Sound actions. Block playback Waits for this sample, including its loops, to finish before the shared audio queue processes the next request. Blocking delay (ms) Displayed as an extra pause after a blocking sound. The current playback path does not apply it. Stop Playback mode Clears pending sound events and requests a stop of active shared audio. It is not limited to one action or device.

Block playback controls the audio queue; it does not make the rest of the profile wait. It also does not retroactively wait for earlier sounds that were started without blocking. A queued Stop previous audio request waits behind any blocking playback already being processed.

Stopping the profile stops shared playback. Inside a Sequence container, the action also requests a shared stop when it receives an end-of-sequence notification. Give the sequence enough duration for its clips to finish; reaching a Play Sound step alone does not wait for the audio.

Stop Playback uses the action's trigger settings, but hides the detailed options panel. Configure the trigger edge before switching to Stop Playback if you need something other than the default press trigger, and review its saving limitation below.

docs.title: Suppress duplicate speech
docs.text:
Suppress Duplicate Playback skips a TTS request when its phrase matches the immediately preceding accepted phrase and the cooldown has not expired. New actions inherit the application's suppression defaults; the configuration defaults are enabled with a 5-second cooldown.

The cooldown control displays seconds, despite the adjacent Delay (ms) label in the current layout. Suppression is separate from Timed Random: randomization chooses a phrase, then duplicate suppression can reject it. It does not prevent the repetitions within one accepted Loops request, and a different intervening phrase changes which phrase counts as the last one.

Disable suppression when every trigger must be heard. For an alternate-phrase test, leave it off until selection works as expected. Audio-file requests use temporary phrase identities, so do not rely on this option as a cooldown for repeatedly triggering the same WAV file.

docs.title: Apply settings across the profile
docs.text:
The device Sync All control and the Sync buttons beside blocking, trimming, and duplicate suppression affect multiple Play Sound actions. Review the destination actions after using them.

The current implementation copies these fields:

Control What is copied to existing actions Device Sync All Stored playback-device name; the follow-default checkbox remains unchanged. Blocking Sync Blocking-delay value; the Block playback checkbox is not copied. Silence Trim Sync All/End trim flags; each action's threshold remains unchanged. Duplicate-suppression Sync Suppression enabled flag. The intended cooldown copy uses a different property, so verify and set each action's actual cooldown.

Some Sync operations also update application defaults. Save the profile after applying changes you want to retain.

docs.title: Play a confirmation sound
docs.text:
1. Add Play Sound/TTS to the confirmation button and select Audio file.
  2. Select a short WAV file, set Volume to 60, and Loops to 1.
  3. Use system-default output and press-only execution.
  4. Leave maximum playback and fades at 0, and leave blocking and Stop previous audio off.
  5. Preview, then start the profile and test one press followed by several rapid presses.

Each accepted press requests a sound. Enable Stop previous audio if a new confirmation should replace one still playing.

docs.title: Speak one of several acknowledgements
docs.text:
1. Select TTS (local) or AI (Edge-TTS), then choose a voice.
  2. Enter Confirmed.|Acknowledged.|Done. in Text.
  3. Select Generate and verify that three phrases are generated.
  4. Select Random under Multi mode and disable Suppress Duplicate Playback for the first test.
  5. Use press-only execution and trigger several times.

One phrase plays per trigger. Choose Round Robin for an ordered cycle or Timed Random to prefer recently unused alternatives.

docs.title: Send announcements to a headset
docs.text:
1. Disable Use system default playback device.
  2. Select the headset in Playback device.
  3. Preview the sound, then change the Windows default device and preview again.
  4. Keep ordinary feedback actions on the system default if they should use another output.

Check the headset connection before relying on the route: a missing fixed device can cause fallback to the default output.

docs.title: Play two announcements in order
docs.text:
1. Create two Play Sound/TTS actions with short clips or generated phrases.
  2. Enable Block playback on the first action and keep Stop previous audio off on the second.
  3. Trigger the first action, then the second.

The second queued sound waits for the first blocking clip to finish. Other profile mappings continue running. If these actions are in a Sequence container, allow enough sequence time for the audio, since the sequence's end notification can stop shared playback. Blocking delay is not currently an added pause between them.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom Check No sound in preview File exists; selected output available; action and Windows volume; Loops at least 1; maximum playback at 0; Silence Trim set to None for diagnosis. Preview works but the input does not Profile running; correct mode; enabled action/container; trigger edge; conditions; hat virtual-button directions. Sound plays twice per button cycle Both trigger edges enabled, duplicate mappings, or a container generating repeated events. Source release does not stop the sound Expected for a press-triggered request; playback is not tied to the source hold duration. New sounds overlap Disable overlapping through the appropriate Block playback or Stop previous audio behavior. Later sound requests are delayed A blocking clip or its loops is still running; generation or conversion may also be pending. Repeated speech is missing Suppress Duplicate Playback and its cooldown. A folder sample repeats The selection pool may be exhausted within its cooldown; reuse is then allowed. Speech generation fails Nonempty text; installed local voice, or Edge voice/network connection; FFmpeg availability/conversion; writable managed sounds folder; log details. First trigger is slow Generate and preview the phrases ahead of use, or export a static WAV. Dynamic text can require a new phrase. Speech wording changes or characters disappear Text sanitation removes parenthesized/backtick content and replaces unsupported characters. Preview the final audio. Sound goes to another device Follow-default checkbox, fixed endpoint availability, Windows default output, and fallback warning in the log. A quiet sound or syllable is missing Disable Silence Trim, then lower its threshold if trimming is needed. Nonzero maximum playback cuts off too soon The current editor has a seconds/milliseconds conversion issue. Leave it at 0 and use a prepared shorter clip. Audio stops when a sequence ends Play Sound reacts to end-of-sequence notifications by requesting a shared stop. Review sequence duration and overlapping actions. A synced setting differs on another action Review the fields actually copied by each Sync control.

Start diagnosis with Audio file mode, a known-good WAV, default output, one loop, no fades, no duration limit, no trim, and press-only execution. Add speech generation, randomization, and queue controls after that test works.

docs.title: Sequence Container — User Guide
docs.text:
The Sequence container runs groups of GremlinEx actions as a series of steps. Use it for a command sequence, a loop, one step per trigger, or a random choice of commands. Each step can contain one or more actions, including a Macro action.

The container controls when steps receive press and release events. The actions inside each step determine the actual output, such as a keyboard shortcut, a virtual joystick button, an OSC message, or a sound.

docs.title: Contents
docs.text:
• Before you start
  • Create your first sequence
  • Add and arrange steps
  • Choose an execution mode
  • Normal: run once
  • Toggle: start and stop a loop
  • Loop: run while pressed
  • Wiggle: vary the steps and timing
  • Step: advance once per trigger
  • Choose the triggering event
  • Set step timing and repetition
  • Sequence timing
  • Per-step repeat options
  • Set startup and resume behavior
  • Conditions and action behavior
  • Runtime settings
  • Worked examples
  • Send two virtual button commands in order
  • Toggle a repeating sequence
  • Choose one random command
  • Cycle commands one press at a time
  • Troubleshooting

docs.title: Before you start
docs.text:
Have a profile containing the source input and a way to observe the output. For virtual joystick output, use the input viewer or a joystick monitor before testing in a game.

The container declares support for joystick buttons and hats. Configure a hat's virtual-button activation directions so it supplies a pressed/released state. Other input types depend on how the surrounding input configuration presents them; do not assume Sequence can be added directly to a raw axis.

For the first test, use a button, two simple actions, execution on press only, and Normal (run once) mode. Keep mode-changing actions outside the sequence: runtime settings can delay a mode change or terminate the running sequence.

docs.title: Create your first sequence
docs.text:
1. Select the profile mode and source input.
  2. Choose Sequence in the Container selector and add it.
  3. Select an action in the container's action selector and click Add Step. Configure its output.
  4. Add a second step with another easy-to-observe output.
  5. Select Normal (run once) under Execution mode.
  6. Enable Execute on press, disable Execute on release, and leave Continue on trigger reset enabled.
  7. Set Step Autorelease delay (ms) to 125 and Step Interval Delay (ms) to 300 for the initial test.
  8. Save and start the profile. Press the source once and observe the two outputs in order.

These timing values are examples. They give the target application time to detect each command and make the step order easy to see.

docs.title: Add and arrange steps
docs.text:
A step is an action set, displayed as Step 1, Step 2, and so on.

  • Add Step creates a new step containing the selected action.
  • Use a step's own action controls to add more actions to that step.
  • Use the up, down, top, and bottom controls to change the step order.
  • Use the step's delete control to remove it.
  • Configure each step's Repeat Mode and timing options separately.

Put commands in separate steps when their order or spacing matters. Actions grouped in one step receive the same synthetic press/release cycle; the normal action execution rules still apply within that group.

Recheck repeat counts and timing after reordering or deleting steps. The current implementation stores these options by step position. Empty action sets are omitted from the runnable step list, so give every intended step an action and remove unused empty steps.

docs.title: Choose an execution mode
docs.text:
Execution mode What starts it What it runs What stops it Normal (run once) A selected press or release event. All steps once, in order. End of the sequence, or trigger reset if continuation is disabled. Toggle A selected trigger event. All steps repeatedly, in order. The next selected trigger event. Loop (while pressed) The selected trigger becomes active. All steps repeatedly, in order. The trigger resets. With press-only execution, this is the source release. Wiggle (random) A selected trigger event. Ordered or randomly selected steps, with optional random timing and a step-count limit. The count limit, or trigger reset if continuation is disabled. Step Each selected trigger event. One step, including that step's repeats. Completion of that step, or trigger reset. The next trigger advances to the following step.

Stopping the profile stops any active sequence. Mode changes can also affect execution; see Runtime settings.

docs.title: Normal: run once
docs.text:
Normal starts at Step 1 and runs through the list once. Triggers received while the sequence is already running are ignored rather than queued.

Continue on trigger reset is enabled for new containers. With press-only execution, this allows a quick tap to start the sequence and releasing the source does not interrupt it. Disable continuation when releasing the source should cancel the remaining steps.

docs.title: Toggle: start and stop a loop
docs.text:
The first qualifying trigger starts the loop. The next qualifying trigger stops it. With execution on press only, press once to start and press again to stop; releases do not toggle the loop.

Enable Resume at last step to resume from the stored step position on the next activation. Leave it off to restart at Step 1.

docs.title: Loop: run while pressed
docs.text:
With Execute on press enabled and Execute on release disabled, the sequence loops while the source is held and stops on release. Enable Resume at last step if the next hold should continue from the stored position.

Use this mode for an ordered repeating sequence controlled by a held button or maintained switch. The container does not expose Continue on trigger reset in this mode.

docs.title: Wiggle: vary the steps and timing
docs.text:
Wiggle can vary the order, interval, and number of selected steps independently.

Setting Effect Randomize Steps Picks a step independently for each selection. A step can be selected again immediately; this is not a shuffle that uses every step once. Random Delay Chooses the interval between step selections using Min Delay and Max Delay when the bounds differ. Min Delay (ms) / Max Delay (ms) Bounds for the random interval. Step Interval Delay (ms) Fixed interval when random delay is off or its bounds are equal. Step Autorelease Delay (ms) Default time between a step's press and release. Random Step Count Limits one run to a selected number of step visits. Wiggle Step Count Min / Max Bounds for the number of step visits in a limited run. Continue on trigger reset Allows the current run to continue after the source changes state. Resume at last step Reuses the stored step position when restarting an ordered run. Randomize Steps picks a new random starting step.

To run only while held, disable Continue on trigger reset and use press-only execution. With continuation enabled and no step-count limit, releasing the source does not stop Wiggle; stop the profile to end it.

With Randomize Steps off, steps run in their displayed order and wrap to Step 1. With Random Step Count off, there is no count-based stop.

For a fixed number of selections, enable Random Step Count and set Min and Max to the same positive value. For example, 3 and 3 select three steps before stopping. Each selected step still applies its own repeat options: one step visit can produce several output pulses, or none when its random repeat count is zero.

In this implementation, unequal Wiggle delay and step-count bounds use an exclusive maximum. A count range of 2 to 5 selects 2, 3, or 4 visits. Equal count bounds select that exact count. Equal delay bounds use Step Interval Delay, so set that field explicitly when you want a fixed interval.

docs.title: Step: advance once per trigger
docs.text:
Step mode runs one step on each qualifying trigger. After the final step, the next trigger wraps to Step 1. Any repeats configured on that step run before it finishes.

Reset step execution on profile start resets the current position to Step 1. It is enabled for new containers. When disabled, the current runtime position can be retained across profile stop/start; it is not a saved progress marker for reopening the profile or application.

A new trigger does not queue another step while the current step is still running. With press-only execution, releasing the source can interrupt the active step's remaining repeats. Test complete press/release cycles at the speed you intend to use.

docs.title: Choose the triggering event
docs.text:
Execute on press and Execute on release choose which source events count as active triggers. New containers use press only.

Selection Consequence Press only Normal choice for a button: press starts or advances; release resets the trigger. Release only Source release starts or advances. The next source press is a trigger reset. Both Both edges qualify. Step can advance twice per physical cycle; Toggle can start on press and stop on release. Loop does not get its usual release reset. Neither Source events do not start the sequence.

Continue on trigger reset is shown in Normal and Wiggle modes. It suppresses further source state changes while that run is active. It does not enable simultaneous runs of the same container, override profile stop, or change mode-affinity settings.

The trigger settings on an action inside a step are separate from the container's trigger settings. The container can start on source release while still sending a synthetic press followed by a release to each step.

docs.title: Set step timing and repetition
docs.text: All delay fields use milliseconds: 1000 ms is one second.

docs.title: Sequence timing
docs.text:
The standard step cycle is:

  1. Send a press to the step's actions.
  2. Wait for the autorelease delay.
  3. Send a release to the step's actions.
  4. Repeat the same step if configured, waiting its repeat delay between repetitions.
  5. Wait the sequence's interval before the next step.

In Normal mode, the container does not add a trailing interval after the final step. Toggle and Loop apply the interval when wrapping to Step 1. Wiggle applies its interval after each selected step, including the final selection of a count-limited run.

Setting New-container default Use Normal Step Interval Delay 0 ms Gap after one step's release and before the next step's press. Normal Step Autorelease delay 250 ms Time between a step's press and release when its Repeat Mode is No Repeat. Wiggle Step Interval Delay 250 ms Fixed gap between selected steps. Wiggle Step Autorelease Delay 250 ms Default press duration for a selected step. Wiggle Random Delay Enabled; 250 to 5000 ms Random gap instead of the fixed Wiggle interval when the bounds differ.

The standard timing controls are displayed in Normal mode. Toggle, Loop, and Step reuse those stored values even though the controls are hidden. Select Normal to adjust them, then switch back to the intended mode. Step uses the autorelease duration and repeat settings; it does not wait an additional interval for another source trigger.

For example, an autorelease delay of 125 ms and interval of 300 ms place the second step's press about 425 ms after the first step's press, plus action execution time. These are scheduled delays, not a guarantee of exact timing in the target application.

docs.title: Per-step repeat options
docs.text:
Each step has its own Repeat Mode:

Repeat Mode Number of press/release cycles per visit No Repeat One. Uses the sequence mode's default timing. Repeat (roundrobin) Exactly Count cycles of this same step. Count includes the first execution. Repeat (random) A random number from zero through Count, inclusive. Zero skips the step's normal press/release cycles.

The repeat modes expose these additional controls:

  • Count: total fixed count or maximum random count. The editor starts at 2.
  • Repeat delay (ms): gap between one repetition's release and the next repetition's press.
  • Autorelease delay (ms): time between each repetition's press and release.
  • Randomize beside either delay: uses that delay's Min and Max fields. These per-step random bounds include both endpoints.

New per-step repeat and autorelease delays are 250 ms. Enabling a repeat mode uses those per-step values instead of the sequence's default duration. Keep each Min less than or equal to its Max.

Repeating a step repeats all actions in that step. Repeat (roundrobin) does not alternate between different steps. Use separate steps and Toggle or Loop for that behavior.

docs.title: Set startup and resume behavior
docs.text:
State on profile start offers two choices:

Choice Behavior Ignore Waits for a new source event. This is the default. Input For a joystick button, reads its current state when the profile starts and processes it using the container's trigger settings.

With Input and press-only execution, a switch already on can start the sequence immediately. With release-only execution, a button already released can trigger startup execution. Hat startup synchronization is not implemented in this container; do not rely on Input to start from a held hat direction.

Resume at last step is available in Toggle, Loop, and Wiggle. It resumes from a stored step position, rather than from the middle of a press or repeat delay. It is not progress saved into the profile file, and a profile mode change clears the stored resume position. Random step selection can choose a different step regardless of that position.

In Step mode, use Reset step execution on profile start to control the step cursor. After switching execution modes or changing the step list, restart and test the first step to confirm the desired startup behavior.

docs.title: Conditions and action behavior
docs.text:
Container conditions determine whether a source event reaches the Sequence container. Step/action conditions and each action's own execution settings also affect the output when a step is visited. A step that produces no output can still consume timing and a step-count visit.

Keep trigger-reset events able to reach a running Loop or cancellable sequence. A condition that allows the initiating press but blocks its release can prevent the expected stop event from reaching the container.

The events sent to steps are synthetic button press and release events. Actions should be configured for that behavior. For example, a normal Hold mapping can use the synthetic release, while an explicit Press, Toggle, or timed Pulse action manages its output differently. See the Map to vJoy guide and Keyboard Ex guide for their output modes.

Sequence controls step dispatch and timing. An action that starts its own background work, such as a macro or sound, may continue after its step has been dispatched. Allow enough time for the intended output and check that action's stop behavior; step order alone does not guarantee that every background effect has finished before the next step begins.

When stopped during an autorelease wait, the container still sends the active step its release event. Normal, Toggle, and Loop also send end-of-sequence release notifications to the steps. Outputs deliberately latched by Press or Toggle actions still need the matching action behavior to clear them.

docs.title: Runtime settings
docs.text:
The application's Runtime Options affect all Sequence containers:

Setting Effect Concurrent sequence limit Maximum number of Sequence runners active at once. 0 means no global limit. A start rejected by the limit is not queued. Mode change aborts running macros/sequences Allows a mode change immediately rather than waiting for active sequences to finish. Sequence/Macro mode affinity Stops a running sequence when the runtime profile mode changes.

Each individual Sequence container can have only one active runner regardless of the global limit. If mode changes wait for sequences to finish, an indefinite Toggle, Loop, or Wiggle run must stop before a waiting mode change can proceed. Keep mode changes outside the sequence and test the chosen runtime settings together.

docs.title: Send two virtual button commands in order
docs.text:
1. Add Sequence to a joystick button and select Normal.
  2. Add a Map to vJoy action in Step 1, targeting virtual button 1 with normal Hold behavior.
  3. Add another in Step 2, targeting virtual button 2 with Hold behavior.
  4. Leave both steps on No Repeat. Set autorelease to 125 ms and interval to 300 ms.
  5. Use press-only execution with Continue on trigger reset enabled.
  6. Start the profile and tap the source once.

Button 1 turns on, releases, and then button 2 turns on and releases. Bind the two virtual buttons in the target application after verifying the order in a monitor.

docs.title: Toggle a repeating sequence
docs.text:
1. Configure the two steps above.
  2. In Normal mode, set autorelease to 125 ms and interval to 500 ms.
  3. Switch to Toggle, use press-only execution, and leave Resume at last step off.
  4. Start the profile. Press once to repeat the two commands and press again to stop.

The next activation starts at Step 1. Enable Resume at last step if continuing from the stored step position is preferable.

docs.title: Choose one random command
docs.text:
1. Create one step per possible command and leave each on No Repeat.
  2. Select Wiggle and enable Randomize Steps.
  3. Enable Random Step Count and set both Min and Max to 1.
  4. Disable Random Delay and set Step Interval Delay to 0 ms.
  5. Set Step Autorelease Delay to 125 ms.
  6. Use press-only execution and enable Continue on trigger reset so a quick tap can finish the selected command.

Each trigger runs one randomly chosen step and stops. Consecutive triggers may choose the same step.

docs.title: Cycle commands one press at a time
docs.text:
1. Add three steps with different outputs and leave each on No Repeat.
  2. In Normal mode, set the desired autorelease duration, such as 125 ms.
  3. Select Step and enable Reset step execution on profile start.
  4. Use press-only execution, start the profile, and test three presses followed by a fourth.

The first three triggers run Steps 1, 2, and 3. The fourth wraps to Step 1. Test the source's release timing as well, since releasing can shorten the active pulse.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
Symptom Check Sequence is unavailable for the selected input Use a supported button or hat input and check its input-type configuration. Nothing happens Profile running; correct profile mode; enabled container/actions; trigger selection; conditions; nonempty steps; valid output target. Only the first command runs after a quick tap Enable Continue on trigger reset in Normal or Wiggle if release should not cancel the run. Wiggle continues after release Disable Continue on trigger reset for held operation, or use Random Step Count for a bounded run. Toggle starts and stops during one press/release cycle Select only one trigger edge. Step advances twice Both Execute on press and Execute on release may be enabled. Rapid triggers are missed The same container is still running its current step or sequence; triggers are not queued. Review autorelease, repeats, and intervals. Repeated step is skipped occasionally Repeat (random) can choose zero. Use No Repeat or Repeat (roundrobin) when it must execute. A random command occurs twice in succession Expected: Randomize Steps selects independently each time. Wiggle never uses the displayed maximum count Unequal Wiggle count bounds exclude Max. Use equal bounds for an exact count. Equal Wiggle delay bounds do not give the desired delay Set Step Interval Delay; equal bounds use that fixed interval. Timing controls disappear Normal timing controls are hidden in Toggle, Loop, and Step. Switch to Normal to edit the stored values. A command activates unexpectedly at startup Set State on profile start to Ignore, or review Input synchronization and the trigger edge. A mode change waits indefinitely Stop the active loop and review Mode change aborts running macros/sequences and mode affinity. A sequence does not start while others run Review Concurrent sequence limit. The log reports SEQUENCE: exceeded concurrent sequence limit when a start is rejected. Output stays pressed or background work overlaps Review the action's Hold/Press/Toggle/Pulse behavior, its release handling, and any independent macro or sound timing. Timing changes after rearranging steps Review repeat and delay options at each step position and remove empty action sets.

For diagnosis, start with Normal mode, two simple steps, No Repeat, and visible delays. Verify the source event, then the step output, and then the target application's binding. Add repetition, conditions, and randomization after that test works.

docs.title: State Device — User Guide
docs.text:
Use the State Device to create named on/off values in a GremlinEx profile. A state can record a switch position, enable a group of commands, combine several inputs, or trigger a shared mapping.

Create the states in the State Device tab, change ordinary states with Map to State, and use their values in conditions or mappings. State definitions belong to the saved profile. Their runtime values are available across the profile's modes.

docs.text:
